nodes.name: Probability density f
nodes.statement: Let $f : \mathbb{R}^d \to (0, \infty)$ be a probability density.
nodes.section: 3 Problem setup and the canonical diffusion

nodes.name: Generator spectrum of a reversible diffusion
nodes.statement: A reversible It\^o diffusion with stationary density $f$ has a self-adjoint generator $\mathcal{L}_f$ on $L^2(f\,dx)$ with discrete spectrum $0 = \mu_1 < \mu_2 \leq \mu_3 \leq \cdots$ and orthonormal eigenfunctions $\{\psi_k\}$; small eigenvalues correspond to slow relaxation modes, each reflecting a barrier the process crosses rarely, so the number and magnitude of near-zero eigenvalues encode the metastable structure of $f$~\cite{Pavliotis2014}.
nodes.section: 3 Problem setup and the canonical diffusion
nodes.statement_short: A reversible diffusion with stationary f has a self-adjoint generator with discrete spectrum $0=\mu_1<\mu_2\le\cdots$; small eigenvalues encode barriers.

nodes.name: Canonical diffusion
nodes.statement: We single out a specific diffusion by reversibility with respect to $f$ and constant scalar diffusion $A_0 = \sigma_f^2 I_d$, $\sigma_f^2 = \mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{Cov}_f(X))/d$, giving the \emph{canonical diffusion} of $f$: \begin{equation} dX_t \;=\; \tfrac12\,\sigma_f^2\,\nabla \log f(X_t)\,dt \;+\; \sigma_f\,dW_t, \end{equation} with $W_t$ a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion.
nodes.section: 3 Problem setup and the canonical diffusion
nodes.statement_short: The reversible diffusion with stationary density f and diffusion $\sigma_f^2 I_d$, $\sigma_f^2=\mathrm{tr}\,\mathrm{Cov}_f/d$: Langevin SDE with drift $\tfrac12\sigma_f^2\nabla\log f$.

nodes.name: Canonical diffusion SDE
nodes.statement: dX_t \;=\; \tfrac12\,\sigma_f^2\,\nabla \log f(X_t)\,dt \;+\; \sigma_f\,dW_t,
nodes.section: 3 Problem setup and the canonical diffusion
nodes.label: eq:canonical_sde

nodes.name: Uniqueness of the canonical diffusion
nodes.statement: Fix any $A_0\succ 0$ and let $f$ be sufficiently regular. Among reversible It\^o diffusions with stationary density $f$ and constant diffusion matrix $A_0$, the drift is uniquely $b(x) = \tfrac12 A_0\nabla\log f(x)$. (Detailed assumptions and proof: Appendix~\ref{app:uniqueness_proof}.)
nodes.section: 3 Problem setup and the canonical diffusion
assumptions: Fix any $A_0\succ 0$ and let $f$ be sufficiently regular.
reversible It\^o diffusions with stationary density $f$ and constant diffusion matrix $A_0$
conclusions: the drift is uniquely $b(x) = \tfrac12 A_0\nabla\log f(x)$
nodes.statement_short: The only reversible diffusion with stationary density f and constant diffusion matrix $A_0$ has drift $\tfrac12 A_0\nabla\log f$.
nodes.label: thm:uniqueness

nodes.name: Similarity Invariance
nodes.statement: The canonical diffusion is covariant under similarity transformations: if $Y = cQX + b$ for any $c > 0$, orthogonal $Q$, and $b \in \mathbb{R}^d$, then $Y_t = cQX_t + b$ is the canonical diffusion for the density of $Y$. In particular, the generator spectrum is preserved, so SSA and DA are invariant under rotation, uniform rescaling, and translation. (Proof: Appendix~\ref{app:similarity_proof}.)
nodes.section: 3 Problem setup and the canonical diffusion
assumptions: $Y = cQX + b$ for any $c > 0$, orthogonal $Q$, and $b \in \mathbb{R}^d$
conclusions: $Y_t = cQX_t + b$ is the canonical diffusion for the density of $Y$
the generator spectrum is preserved, so SSA and DA are invariant under rotation, uniform rescaling, and translation
nodes.statement_short: Similarity maps of the data map canonical diffusions to canonical diffusions, so the generator spectrum, SSA and DA are similarity invariant.
nodes.label: prop:similarity_invariance

nodes.name: Robustness to the coefficient choice
nodes.statement: We fix $A_0 = \sigma_f^2 I_d$. For scalar alternatives $A_0 = cI$ ($c>0$), DA directions are unchanged and SSA is invariant (Prop.~\ref{prop:similarity_invariance}). For general $A_0\succ 0$, Rayleigh bounds (App.~\ref{app:robustness}) control slow-eigenvalue shifts, and in the deep-metastable regime barrier-height exponents dominate; DA may depend on $A_0$. The same holds for kinetic Langevin in the deep-barrier limit.
nodes.section: 3 Problem setup and the canonical diffusion
nodes.statement_short: Scalar $A_0=cI$ leaves DA unchanged; for general $A_0$ Rayleigh bounds control slow eigenvalues and barrier exponents dominate in the metastable regime.

nodes.name: Centered canonical process
nodes.statement: Both of our readouts derive from the stationary autocovariance of the centered process $Y_t = X_t - \bar x_f$, where $\bar x_f = \mathbb{E}_f[X]$.
nodes.section: 3 Problem setup and the canonical diffusion

nodes.name: Autocovariance and trace-normalized autocorrelation
nodes.statement: Let $C(\tau) = \mathbb{E}_f[Y_\tau Y_0^\top]$ and $\rho(\tau) = \mathrm{tr} C(\tau) / \mathrm{tr} C(0)$.
nodes.section: 3 Problem setup and the canonical diffusion

nodes.name: Projection coefficients
nodes.statement: Define projection coefficients $\alpha_k = \int (x - \bar x_f)\psi_k(x) f(x)\,dx$, with $\alpha_1 = 0$ since $\psi_1 \equiv 1$.
nodes.section: 3 Problem setup and the canonical diffusion

nodes.name: Trajectory-averaged lag-tau autocovariance estimator
nodes.statement: The empirical estimator from $N$ canonical-diffusion trajectories of length $T+1$ (simulated via the score; Algorithm~\ref{alg:ssa_da}) is the trajectory-averaged lag-$\tau$ cross product \begin{equation} \hat C(\tau) \;:=\; \frac{1}{N(T+1-\tau)} \sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{t=0}^{T-\tau} (X_t^{(n)} - \bar x)(X_{t+\tau}^{(n)} - \bar x)^\top, \end{equation} with $\bar x = (1/[N(T+1)]) \sum_{n,t} X_t^{(n)}$, and $\hat C^{\mathrm{sym}}(\tau) = \tfrac{1}{2}[\hat C(\tau) + \hat C(\tau)^\top]$.
nodes.section: 3 Problem setup and the canonical diffusion
nodes.statement_short: Estimator $\hat C(\tau)$: lag-$\tau$ cross products of centered points averaged over N trajectories; $\hat C^{\mathrm{sym}}$ is its symmetric part.

nodes.name: Empirical autocovariance
nodes.statement: \hat C(\tau) \;:=\; \frac{1}{N(T+1-\tau)} \sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{t=0}^{T-\tau} (X_t^{(n)} - \bar x)(X_{t+\tau}^{(n)} - \bar x)^\top,
nodes.section: 3 Problem setup and the canonical diffusion
nodes.label: eq:c_hat_def

nodes.name: Spectral representation of C(tau)
nodes.statement: The stationary autocovariance satisfies: \[ C(\tau) = \sum_{k \geq 2} e^{-\mu_k \tau}\,\alpha_k \alpha_k^\top, \quad \rho(\tau) = \sum_{k \geq 2} e^{-\mu_k \tau}\, w_k, \quad w_k = \tfrac{\|\alpha_k\|^2}{\sum_{j \geq 2}\|\alpha_j\|^2} \]
nodes.section: 3 Problem setup and the canonical diffusion
conclusions: C(\tau) = \sum_{k \geq 2} e^{-\mu_k \tau}\,\alpha_k \alpha_k^\top
\rho(\tau) = \sum_{k \geq 2} e^{-\mu_k \tau}\, w_k
nodes.statement_short: $C(\tau)$ is a sum of rank-one terms $e^{-\mu_k\tau}\alpha_k\alpha_k^\top$, so $\rho(\tau)$ is a mixture of exponentials with weights $w_k$.
nodes.label: lem:spectral

nodes.name: SSA (Sum of Squared Autocorrelations)
nodes.statement: The SSA of $f$ is \begin{equation} S(f) \;:=\; \int_0^\infty \rho(\tau)^2\,d\tau. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 SSA: a scalar measure of mode separation
nodes.statement_short: SSA $S(f)$ is the integral of $\rho(\tau)^2$ over all lags.
nodes.label: def:ssa

nodes.name: SSA definition
nodes.statement: S(f) \;:=\; \int_0^\infty \rho(\tau)^2\,d\tau.
nodes.section: 4 SSA: a scalar measure of mode separation
nodes.label: eq:ssa_score

nodes.name: Spectral formula for SSA
nodes.statement: $S(f) \;=\; \displaystyle\sum_{k,\ell \geq 2} \frac{w_k w_\ell}{\mu_k + \mu_\ell}$, with the convention $1/0 = +\infty$. $S(f)<\infty$ whenever the canonical diffusion has a spectral gap. (Proof: Appendix~\ref{app:spectral}.)
nodes.section: 4 SSA: a scalar measure of mode separation
assumptions: whenever the canonical diffusion has a spectral gap
conclusions: $S(f) \;=\; \displaystyle\sum_{k,\ell \geq 2} \frac{w_k w_\ell}{\mu_k + \mu_\ell}$
$S(f)<\infty$
nodes.statement_short: $S(f)=\sum_{k,\ell} w_k w_\ell/(\mu_k+\mu_\ell)$, finite under a spectral gap.
nodes.label: thm:ssa_spectral

nodes.name: Monotonicity of SSA in every eigenvalue
nodes.statement: In the spectral formula of Corollary~\ref{thm:ssa_spectral}, holding the weights $\{w_k\}_{k\ge 2}$ and all other eigenvalues fixed, $S(f)$ is nonincreasing in each generator eigenvalue $\mu_k$, and strictly decreasing in $\mu_k$ whenever $w_k > 0$. The same holds for the finite-horizon score $S_T(f) = \int_0^T \rho(\tau)^2\,d\tau$. (Proof: differentiate spectral formula from Corollary~\ref{thm:ssa_spectral}; Appendix~\ref{app:monotonicity_proof}.)
nodes.section: 4 SSA: a scalar measure of mode separation
assumptions: holding the weights $\{w_k\}_{k\ge 2}$ and all other eigenvalues fixed
conclusions: $S(f)$ is nonincreasing in each generator eigenvalue $\mu_k$, and strictly decreasing in $\mu_k$ whenever $w_k > 0$
The same holds for the finite-horizon score $S_T(f) = \int_0^T \rho(\tau)^2\,d\tau$.
nodes.statement_short: With weights fixed, SSA (and its finite-horizon version) decreases in every generator eigenvalue.
nodes.label: prop:ssa_monotonicity

nodes.name: SSA for k well-separated equal-weight modes
nodes.statement: Suppose $f$ has $k$ equally weighted, well-separated modes with all inter-mode barriers of common height $\Delta U$ (so the $k-1$ slow eigenvalues are all approximately $\mu_{\mathrm{slow}} \sim e^{-\Delta U}$ and the slow-mode variance fraction is $(k-1)/k$). Then $S(f) \approx (k-1)^2 / (2 k^2 \mu_{\mathrm{slow}}) + O(1/\mu_{\mathrm{fast}})$, monotone in $\Delta U$ and saturating at $1/(2\mu_{\mathrm{slow}})$ as $k \to \infty$. (Proof: direct evaluation of Corollary~\ref{thm:ssa_spectral} at the assumed spectral profile.)
nodes.section: 4 SSA: a scalar measure of mode separation
assumptions: $f$ has $k$ equally weighted, well-separated modes with all inter-mode barriers of common height $\Delta U$
the $k-1$ slow eigenvalues are all approximately $\mu_{\mathrm{slow}} \sim e^{-\Delta U}$ and the slow-mode variance fraction is $(k-1)/k$
conclusions: $S(f) \approx (k-1)^2 / (2 k^2 \mu_{\mathrm{slow}}) + O(1/\mu_{\mathrm{fast}})$
monotone in $\Delta U$ and saturating at $1/(2\mu_{\mathrm{slow}})$ as $k \to \infty$
nodes.statement_short: For k equal modes with common barrier, $S\approx (k-1)^2/(2k^2\mu_{slow})$: growing with barrier height, saturating in k.
nodes.label: prop:ssa_k_modes

nodes.name: SSA weighs slow modes by variance share
nodes.statement: SSA summarizes slow-mode dynamics weighted by their variance share, not the number of modes (illustrated by Figure~\ref{fig:gmm_sweeps} (d)). Proposition~\ref{prop:ssa_monotonicity} is therefore a statement about the spectral formula with fixed weights, not a claim that every density deformation that deepens a barrier must increase SSA.
nodes.section: 4 SSA: a scalar measure of mode separation
nodes.statement_short: SSA reflects slow modes weighted by variance share, not mode count; monotonicity is only at fixed weights.

nodes.name: Empirical SSA estimator
nodes.statement: We estimate SSA from $N$ trajectories with step-size $\Delta t$ and horizon $T_{\max}$: \begin{equation} \widehat S \;:=\; \Delta t \sum_{\ell = 0}^{L_{\max}} \hat\rho(\ell\,\Delta t)^2, \end{equation} where $L_{\max} = \lfloor T_{\max}/\Delta t \rfloor$, with $\hat\rho(\tau_\ell) = \mathrm{tr}\hat C(\tau_\ell)/\mathrm{tr}\hat C(0)$ at lag $\tau_\ell = \ell\,\Delta t$.
nodes.section: 4 SSA: a scalar measure of mode separation

nodes.name: SSA estimator
nodes.statement: \widehat S \;:=\; \Delta t \sum_{\ell = 0}^{L_{\max}} \hat\rho(\ell\,\Delta t)^2,
nodes.section: 4 SSA: a scalar measure of mode separation
nodes.label: eq:ssa_estimator

nodes.name: Variance-scale stopping lag T_max
nodes.statement: A principled stopping lag is the largest $\tau$ at which $\hat\rho(\tau)^2$ exceeds the null variance of the trace-normalized estimator under the hypothesis $X_0 \perp X_\tau$: \begin{equation} T_{\max} \;=\; \max\!\left\{\tau \,:\, \hat\rho(\tau)^2 \;>\; \frac{1}{N}\right\}, \end{equation} with $1/N$ a distribution-free upper bound on the asymptotic null variance of $\hat\rho(\tau)$ that holds for any $f$ with finite fourth moments (derivation in Appendix~\ref{app:rho_clt}).
nodes.section: 4 SSA: a scalar measure of mode separation
nodes.statement_short: Stop the SSA lag integral at the largest lag where $\hat\rho^2$ exceeds the distribution-free null-variance bound $1/N$.

nodes.name: Stopping rule T_max
nodes.statement: T_{\max} \;=\; \max\!\left\{\tau \,:\, \hat\rho(\tau)^2 \;>\; \frac{1}{N}\right\},
nodes.section: 4 SSA: a scalar measure of mode separation
nodes.label: eq:tmax_stopping

nodes.name: Dominant Autocorrelation (DA) directions
nodes.statement: For each lag $\tau > 0$, let \[ C(\tau) = \sum_{j=1}^d \lambda_j(\tau)\, v_j(\tau) v_j(\tau)^\top, \qquad \lambda_1(\tau) \geq \lambda_2(\tau) \geq \cdots \geq \lambda_d(\tau), \] be the eigendecomposition of the population autocovariance. The DA directions at lag $\tau$ are the eigenvectors $v_1(\tau), v_2(\tau), \ldots, v_d(\tau)$, ordered by decreasing eigenvalue.
nodes.label: def:da

nodes.name: Convergence of the leading DA direction
nodes.statement: If $\mu_2 < \mu_3$ and $\|\alpha_2\| > 0$, the leading unit-norm eigenvector $v_1(\tau)$ of $C(\tau)$ satisfies $1 - \langle v_1(\tau), \alpha_2\rangle^2 / \|\alpha_2\|^2 = O(e^{-2(\mu_3 - \mu_2)\tau})$ as $\tau \to \infty$. (Proof: Appendix~\ref{app:da_convergence_proof}.)
conclusions: the leading unit-norm eigenvector $v_1(\tau)$ of $C(\tau)$ satisfies $1 - \langle v_1(\tau), \alpha_2\rangle^2 / \|\alpha_2\|^2 = O(e^{-2(\mu_3 - \mu_2)\tau})$ as $\tau \to \infty$
nodes.statement_short: Under a gap $\mu_2<\mu_3$, DA1 aligns with $\alpha_2$ at rate $e^{-2(\mu_3-\mu_2)\tau}$.
nodes.label: prop:da_convergence

nodes.name: Subspace convergence of the top-m DA eigenspace
nodes.statement: Assume $\alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_{m+1}$ are linearly independent and $\mu_{m+1} < \mu_{m+2}$. Then the top-$m$ eigenspace of $C(\tau)$ converges to $\mathrm{span}(\alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_{m+1})$ as $\tau \to \infty$ (Appendix~\ref{app:da_convergence_proof}).
conclusions: the top-$m$ eigenspace of $C(\tau)$ converges to $\mathrm{span}(\alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_{m+1})$ as $\tau \to \infty$

nodes.name: Recovery of individual slow modes by DA
nodes.statement: Recovering the individual slow modes as the eigenvectors $v_2(\tau), \ldots, v_m(\tau)$ requires additional gap and non-collinearity conditions on $\{\alpha_k\}$ that we do not establish in general; we validate per-direction recovery empirically per experiment (Section~\ref{sec:exp_molecular}, Appendix~\ref{app:validation}). A theory is left to future work.
nodes.statement_short: When do the individual DA eigenvectors $v_2,\dots,v_m$ recover individual slow modes? Not established; validated only empirically.

nodes.name: Limit spectrum of the symmetrized lag-tau autocovariance under the isotropic Gaussian null
nodes.statement: Let $f = \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2 I_d)$, $\gamma = d/N$, and fix $\tau > 0$. Let $(X_0^{(n)}, X_\tau^{(n)})_{n=1}^N$ be independent stationary OU lag-pairs from the canonical diffusion of $f$ (within each pair, $X_0$ and $X_\tau$ have the OU correlation $e^{-\tau/2}$; pairs are independent across $n$), and define the simple-pair estimator $\widetilde C(\tau) = (1/N) \sum_n X_0^{(n)}(X_\tau^{(n)})^\top$ and $\widetilde C^{\mathrm{sym}}(\tau) = \tfrac12(\widetilde C(\tau) + \widetilde C(\tau)^\top)$. In the proportional regime $d, N \to \infty$ with $d/N \to \gamma \in (0, \infty)$, the empirical spectral distribution of $\widetilde C^{\mathrm{sym}}(\tau)$ converges weakly almost surely to \begin{equation} \mathrm{d}\mu_\tau^\gamma(\lambda) = \max(0, 1 - 2/\gamma)\,\delta_0(\mathrm{d}\lambda) + \tilde\rho_\tau^\gamma(\lambda)\,\mathrm{d}\lambda, \end{equation} where $\tilde\rho_\tau^\gamma$ is the continuous density of total mass $\min(1, 2/\gamma)$ (the normalized continuous density is $\rho_\tau^\gamma := \tilde\rho_\tau^\gamma / \min(1, 2/\gamma)$). Let $c_\pm(\tau) = (\sigma^2/2)(1 \pm e^{-\tau/2})$ and define \begin{equation} a(\tau) = c_+ c_- \gamma^2 \lambda, \quad b(\tau) = \gamma\bigl[c_+ c_- (2-\gamma) + \lambda(c_+ - c_-)\bigr], \quad c(\tau) = (c_+ - c_-)(1 - \gamma) - \lambda. \end{equation} \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=*,nosep] \item \textbf{Edges and support:} the boundary points of the continuous support are real roots of the discriminant quartic \begin{equation} \Delta_\tau(\lambda) \;=\; 18\,a(\tau)\,b(\tau)\,c(\tau) - 4 b(\tau)^3 + b(\tau)^2 c(\tau)^2 - 4 a(\tau)\, c(\tau)^3 - 27 a(\tau)^2 \;=\; 0. \end{equation} We write $\lambda_+(\tau)$ for the largest real root and $\lambda_-(\tau)$ for the smallest; in the supercritical regime $\gamma > 2$, the quartic can have four real roots and the continuous support is two intervals separated by a gap around $0$. \item \textbf{Density:} on the continuous support, $\tilde\rho_\tau^\gamma(\lambda) = -\pi^{-1}\,\mathrm{Im}\,G(\lambda+i0^+)$, where $G$ is the lower-half-plane root of the Stieltjes cubic ($\Delta_\tau$ is its discriminant) \begin{equation} a(\tau)\,G^3 + b(\tau)\,G^2 + c(\tau)\,G + 1 \;=\; 0. \end{equation} \end{enumerate} At $\tau = 0$, $\mu_0^\gamma$ is the standard Marchenko--Pastur law with edge $\lambda_+(0) = \sigma^2(1+\sqrt\gamma)^2$. As $\tau \to \infty$, \begin{equation} \lambda_+(\tau) \to \lambda_+(\infty) = \frac{\sigma^2}{8}\bigl(\sqrt{1+4\gamma}+3\bigr)^{3/2}\sqrt{\sqrt{1+4\gamma}-1}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Operational noise floor
nodes.statement: Under the null $f = \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I_d)$ there are no slow modes, so the spectrum of $\hat C^{\mathrm{sym}}(\tau)$ is finite-sample noise. Theorem~\ref{thm:limit-spectrum} characterizes it, giving $\lambda_+(\tau)$ as a threshold: slow modes persist above it, non-metastable directions decay into it. The proof (Appendix~\ref{app:limit-spectrum}) is for the simple-pair estimator $\widetilde C^{\mathrm{sym}}(\tau)$ with i.i.d.\ lag-pairs; for the trajectory-averaged $\hat C(\tau)$ (overlapping dependent pairs), we use $\lambda_+(\tau)$ as a reference floor and rely on matched Monte-Carlo calibration when the pipeline departs from the simple-pair null. A practical issue is that once $\nabla \log f$ is estimated rather than known, and especially when DA is computed after a nonlinear embedding, the empirical bulk is typically inflated above the idealized null. Section~\ref{sec:exp_synth_validation} verifies $\rho_\tau^\gamma$ and $\lambda_+(\tau)$ against empirical eigenvalue histograms under the exact null. For pretrained generative models we calibrate the floor by a Monte-Carlo null through the full pipeline using a parallel iso-Gaussian score oracle (Section~\ref{sec:score_high_dim}), so null and data share the pipeline biases (Algorithm~\ref{alg:operational_floor}, Appendix~\ref{app:sdxl_elderly}).
nodes.statement_short: $\lambda_+(\tau)$ serves as the DA noise floor; exact only for the simple-pair estimator, so the pipeline is calibrated by a matched Monte-Carlo null.

nodes.name: Lag-selection criterion tau*(m)
nodes.statement: For $m \geq 1$ directions, choose $\tau^*(m)$ as the largest lag at which: (i) each of the top $m$ eigenvalues of $\hat C^{\mathrm{sym}}(\tau)$ rejects the null at level $\alpha$ (Bonferroni-corrected over the $m$ directions), via either the analytic null of Theorem~\ref{thm:limit-spectrum} or a matched Monte Carlo null (Appendix~\ref{app:validation}); (ii) the 1D projection onto each of $v_1, \ldots, v_m$ rejects unimodality under a 1D multimodality test (Hartigan's dip test~\cite{hartigan1985} or Silverman's bandwidth test~\cite{silverman1981}; see Appendix~\ref{app:validation}); and (iii) $\rho(\tau) < 1/e$, a heuristic guard against under-converged short lags (Appendix~\ref{app:lag_selection}).
nodes.statement_short: $\tau^*(m)$: the largest lag where the top-m eigenvalues beat the null (Bonferroni), each projection rejects unimodality, and $\rho<1/e$.

nodes.name: Number of metastable directions
nodes.statement: The number of metastable directions recovered is the maximal $m$ for which $\tau^*(m)$ exists.

nodes.name: Tweedie's identity
nodes.statement: For score-based generative models, Tweedie's identity (derived in Appendix~\ref{app:tweedie}) gives $\nabla \log f_t(x) = -\epsilon_\theta(x, t) / \sigma_t$ at noise level $t$ with schedule variance $\sigma_t^2$; at small $t$ this provides a score oracle for $f$ via a single denoiser pass with no density estimation and no dimensionality barrier.
assumptions: at noise level $t$ with schedule variance $\sigma_t^2$
conclusions: $\nabla \log f_t(x) = -\epsilon_\theta(x, t) / \sigma_t$
nodes.statement_short: The score of the noised marginal equals minus the predicted noise over $\sigma_t$, so a denoiser gives a score oracle.

nodes.name: SSA and DA from a Score Oracle
nodes.statement: \caption{SSA and DA from a Score Oracle} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \State \textbf{Input:} $\nabla \log \hat{f}$, samples from $f$, trajectories $N$, step $\Delta t$, max steps $T$, lag grid $\{\tau_1 < \cdots < \tau_L\}$ \State \textbf{Output:} SSA score $\hat S$; DA directions $\{v_j, \lambda_j\}_{j=1}^d$ \State $\bar x_f \gets \mathbb{E}_f[X]$,\; $\sigma_f^2 \gets \tfrac{1}{d}\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{Cov}_f(X))$; \State sample $X_0^{(n)} \sim f$ for $n = 1, \ldots, N$ \For{$n = 1, \ldots, N$,\; $t = 0, \ldots, T-1$} \Comment{simulate canonical diffusion} \State $X_{t+1}^{(n)} \gets X_t^{(n)} + \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma_f^2\,\nabla \log f(X_t^{(n)})\,\Delta t + \sigma_f \sqrt{\Delta t}\, Z$, \;\; $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_d)$ \EndFor \For{$\ell = 0, 1, \ldots, L$} \Comment{autocovariance and trace-normalized autocorrelation} \State $\hat C(\tau_\ell) \gets \tfrac{1}{N(T+1-\tau_\ell)} \sum_{n,t} (X_t^{(n)} - \bar x_f)(X_{t+\tau_\ell}^{(n)} - \bar x_f)^\top$; \State $\hat\rho(\tau_\ell) \gets \mathrm{tr} \hat C(\tau_\ell)/\mathrm{tr} \hat C(0)$ \EndFor \State $L^* \gets \max\{\ell : \hat\rho(\tau_\ell)^2 > 1/N\}$; \State $\hat S \gets \int_0^{\tau_{L^*}} \hat\rho(\tau)^2\,d\tau$ \Comment{SSA, Appendix~\ref{app:rho_clt}} \State Select $\tau^* \in \{\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_{L}\}$ (Appendix~\ref{app:lag_selection}; operational floor in Algorithm~\ref{alg:operational_floor}); \State $\hat C^{\mathrm{sym}} \gets \tfrac{1}{2}[\hat C(\tau^*) + \hat C(\tau^*)^\top]$ \State Eigendecompose $\hat C^{\mathrm{sym}} = \sum_j \lambda_j\, v_j v_j^\top$, $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \cdots$ \Comment{DA directions} \State \Return $\hat S$,\; $\{v_j, \lambda_j\}_{j=1}^d$ \end{algorithmic}
input: $\nabla \log \hat{f}$, samples from $f$, trajectories $N$, step $\Delta t$, max steps $T$, lag grid $\{\tau_1 < \cdots < \tau_L\}$
nodes.statement_short: Simulate the canonical diffusion by Euler-Maruyama, estimate $\hat C(\tau)$ on a lag grid, integrate $\hat\rho^2$ to the 1/N stop (SSA) and eigendecompose at $\tau^*$ (DA).
nodes.label: alg:ssa_da

nodes.name: Regularity of f for uniqueness
nodes.statement: We assume $f:\mathbb{R}^d \to (0,\infty)$ is smooth, strictly positive, with tails such that integration by parts has no boundary terms.

nodes.name: Generator of an Ito diffusion
nodes.statement: Consider It\^o diffusions on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with generator $\mathcal{L} \varphi(x) = b(x)\cdot \nabla \varphi(x) + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{tr}(A(x) \nabla^2 \varphi(x))$, where $A(x) = \Sigma(x)\Sigma(x)^\top$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1 (uniqueness)
nodes.statement:
For a general diffusion with $A(x)\equiv A_0$ constant, the Fokker--Planck equation is \[ \partial_t p(x,t) = -
abla \cdot (b(x)\,p(x,t)) +  rac{1}{2}\,
abla \cdot  ig(A_0 
abla p(x,t) ig). \] Define the probability current $J_p(x) := b(x)\,p(x) -  rac{1}{2}A_0 
abla p(x)$. Stationarity with density $f$ requires $
abla \cdot J_f(x) = 0$. Reversibility with respect to $f$ is equivalent to the stronger condition $J_f(x)\equiv 0$ (vanishing probability current; standard characterization of reversible diffusions, see~\cite[Ch.~4]{Pavliotis2014}). With $A(x)\equiv A_0$ and $J_f\equiv 0$, we have $0 = b(x)f(x) -  rac{1}{2}A_0
abla f(x)$, so $b(x) =  rac{1}{2}A_0 
abla \log f(x)$, which uniquely determines the drift and hence the diffusion.
nodes.statement_short: Constant $A_0$ in Fokker-Planck; reversibility means zero probability current, which solves for the drift uniquely.

nodes.name: Necessity of both conditions
nodes.statement:
Both reversibility and the constant-diffusion-matrix assumption are needed for uniqueness. Without reversibility, any smooth $f$-divergence-free vector field $u$ satisfying $
abla \cdot (f(x)\,u(x)) = 0$ can be added to the reversible drift, producing $b(x) =  rac{1}{2}A_0 
abla \log f(x) + u(x)$, which yields the same stationary density $f$ but different dynamics. Without fixed $A_0$, if we allow arbitrary $A(x)$ but enforce $J_f\equiv 0$, then $b(x) =  rac{1}{2}
abla \cdot (A(x)) +  rac{1}{2}A(x)
abla \log f(x)$, so every choice of diffusion matrix produces a different reversible diffusion with stationary density $f$.
nodes.statement_short: Without reversibility add an f-divergence-free drift; without fixed $A_0$ every $A(x)$ gives a different reversible diffusion.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1 (similarity invariance)
nodes.statement:
Let $Y = cQX + b$. By change of variables, $Y$ has density \[ f_Y(y) = c^{-d} f\!\left(c^{-1} Q^	op (y - b)ight). \] Applying It\^o's lemma to $Y_t = cQX_t + b$ yields \[ dY_t = 	frac{1}{2} c \sigma_f^2\, Q 
abla_x \log f(X_t)\,dt + c \sigma_f\, Q\,dW_t. \] The scalar variance of $Y$ is $\sigma_Y^2 = c^2 \sigma_f^2$, and the score transforms as $
abla_y \log f_Y(y) =  rac{1}{c} Q 
abla_x \log f(x)$. Substituting gives \[ dY_t = 	frac{1}{2} \sigma_Y^2\, 
abla \log f_Y(Y_t)\,dt + \sigma_Y\,d	ilde{W}_t, \] where $	ilde{W}_t = Q W_t$ is again standard Brownian motion (orthogonal transformations preserve the distribution of $W$). This is exactly the canonical diffusion for $f_Y$. The change-of-variables map $U\varphi(y) := \varphi(c^{-1}Q^	op(y - b))$ is unitary $L^2(f\,dx) 	o L^2(f_Y\,dy)$ (the density Jacobian $f_Y(y)\,dy = f(x)\,dx$ makes $U$ an isometry without further normalization), and intertwines the two generators: $\mathcal{L}_{f_Y} U = U \mathcal{L}_f$. Hence the spectra coincide.
nodes.statement_short: Ito's lemma plus score and variance transformation rules give the canonical SDE for $Y$; a unitary change of variables intertwines the generators.

nodes.name: Why reversibility
nodes.statement: A diffusion with stationary distribution $f$ is not unique in general: for any smooth vector field $u$ satisfying $\nabla \cdot (f(x)\,u(x)) = 0$, the drift $b(x) = \frac{1}{2}A_0 \nabla \log f(x) + u(x)$ yields a different process with the same stationary density. Such divergence-free components $u$ introduce net probability currents that circulate mass around modes, creating rotational dynamics whose mixing rate depends on the choice of $u$ rather than on the barrier structure of $f$ alone. Requiring reversibility ($J_f \equiv 0$) eliminates all such components, ensuring that the only mechanism for transitioning between modes is diffusion against the barriers of $f$. This makes metastability a property of $f$ rather than an artifact of the dynamics.
nodes.statement_short: Non-reversible drifts add circulating currents whose mixing depends on the drift, not the barriers; reversibility removes them.

nodes.name: Why not A_0 = I_d
nodes.section: A.4 Choice of Diffusion Matrix: Why Not $I_d$ or $\mathrm{Cov}_f(X)$
nodes.statement_short: With $A_0=I_d$ rescaling the data changes the drift-to-noise ratio and so SSA: the measure would depend on units.

nodes.name: Why not A_0 = Cov_f(X)
nodes.statement: Full-covariance whitening, $A_0 = \mathrm{Cov}_f(X)$, is a natural alternative that runs the diffusion in coordinates where the marginal covariance is the identity. This corresponds to a stronger invariance principle than ours: the resulting construction is invariant under arbitrary invertible affine transformations of the data, whereas the scalar variance choice $A_0 = \sigma_f^2 I_d$ is invariant only under similarities (rotation, uniform scaling, translation; Proposition~\ref{prop:similarity_invariance}). Both are defensible design choices with different semantics: similarity invariance treats SSA as a property of the density up to change of units, while affine invariance additionally identifies all densities connected by arbitrary linear reparameterizations. We prefer the minimal choice. It matches the intuition that a multimodality measure should be a function of the shape of $f$ up to a change of units, not up to arbitrary linear distortion; it requires estimating a single scalar $\sigma_f^2$ rather than $d(d+1)/2$ parameters; and it remains well defined in the high-dimensional, sample-limited regime (Appendix~\ref{app:noise_floor}), where $\mathrm{Cov}_f(X)$ is typically rank-deficient or ill-conditioned and requires regularization that interpolates back toward the scalar convention.
nodes.section: A.4 Choice of Diffusion Matrix: Why Not $I_d$ or $\mathrm{Cov}_f(X)$
nodes.statement_short: Whitening gives affine invariance but needs $d(d+1)/2$ parameters and fails in the sample-limited regime; the scalar choice is minimal.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1 and of the spectral formula for SSA
nodes.statement: Let $P_\tau = e^{\tau\mathcal{L}_f}$ denote the Markov semigroup generated by $\mathcal{L}_f$. By the Kolmogorov backward equation, $P_\tau$ acts as conditional expectation: $\mathbb{E}_f[\varphi(X_\tau) \mid X_0 = x] = (P_\tau \varphi)(x)$ for any $\varphi \in L^2(f\,dx)$. By the spectral theorem for self-adjoint operators, $\{\psi_k\}_{k \geq 1}$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $L^2(f\,dx)$ and $P_\tau \psi_k = e^{-\mu_k \tau}\psi_k$. The centered coordinate map $g(x) := x - \bar x_f$ is vector-valued; we assume $f$ has finite second moments so that each component $g_j \in L^2(f\,dx)$. Expanding each component in the eigenbasis, \[ g_j(x) = \sum_{k \geq 1} (\alpha_k)_j\, \psi_k(x), \qquad (\alpha_k)_j = \langle g_j, \psi_k\rangle_f = \int (x_j - (\bar x_f)_j)\,\psi_k(x)\,f(x)\,dx. \] Stacking across coordinates gives $g(x) = \sum_{k \geq 1} \alpha_k\,\psi_k(x)$. The $k = 1$ term drops out because $\psi_1 \equiv 1$, so $(\alpha_1)_j = \mathbb{E}_f[X_j] - (\bar x_f)_j = 0$ by the definition of $\bar x_f$. Hence $g = \sum_{k \geq 2}\alpha_k\,\psi_k$ and, applying $P_\tau$ coordinate-wise, \begin{equation} \mathbb{E}_f[g(X_\tau) \mid X_0 = x] = (P_\tau g)(x) = \sum_{k \geq 2} e^{-\mu_k \tau}\,\alpha_k\,\psi_k(x). \end{equation} \textit{(i)} Writing the expectation over the joint stationary distribution of $(X_0, X_\tau)$ and integrating out $X_\tau$ first via the tower property, \[ C(\tau) = \mathbb{E}_f[Y_\tau Y_0^\top] = \int \mathbb{E}_f[Y_\tau \mid X_0 = x]\,(x - \bar x_f)^\top\, f(x)\,dx. \] Substituting~\eqref{eq:cond_exp_expansion} and pulling the sum outside the integral, \[ C(\tau) = \sum_{k \geq 2} e^{-\mu_k \tau}\,\alpha_k \left[\int \psi_k(x)\,(x - \bar x_f)^\top f(x)\,dx\right]. \] The bracketed quantity is a row vector whose $j$-th entry is $\int (x_j - (\bar x_f)_j)\,\psi_k(x)\,f(x)\,dx = (\alpha_k)_j$, i.e., it equals $\alpha_k^\top$. Therefore \[ C(\tau) = \sum_{k \geq 2} e^{-\mu_k \tau}\,\alpha_k\,\alpha_k^\top. \] \textit{(ii)} Taking the trace of (i) and using $\mathrm{tr}(\alpha_k \alpha_k^\top) = \|\alpha_k\|^2$, \[ \mathrm{tr} C(\tau) = \sum_{k \geq 2} e^{-\mu_k \tau}\,\|\alpha_k\|^2. \] At $\tau = 0$, $\mathrm{tr} C(0) = \sum_{k \geq 2}\|\alpha_k\|^2$, so \[ \rho(\tau) = \frac{\mathrm{tr} C(\tau)}{\mathrm{tr} C(0)} = \sum_{k \geq 2} e^{-\mu_k \tau}\,w_k, \qquad w_k := \frac{\|\alpha_k\|^2}{\sum_{j \geq 2}\|\alpha_j\|^2}. \] \textit{(iii) Spectral formula for SSA (Corollary~\ref{thm:ssa_spectral}).} From (ii), $\rho(\tau)^2 = \sum_{k, \ell \geq 2} w_k w_\ell\, e^{-(\mu_k + \mu_\ell)\tau}$. Integrating term-by-term over $[0, \infty)$, \begin{equation} S(f) \;=\; \int_0^\infty \rho(\tau)^2\,d\tau \;=\; \sum_{k,\ell \geq 2} w_k w_\ell \int_0^\infty e^{-(\mu_k+\mu_\ell)\tau}\,d\tau \;=\; \sum_{k,\ell \geq 2} \frac{w_k w_\ell}{\mu_k + \mu_\ell}, \end{equation} which is the spectral formula of Corollary~\ref{thm:ssa_spectral}.
nodes.statement_short: Expand the centered coordinates in the generator eigenbasis and apply the semigroup; trace and integrate term by term.

nodes.name: Conditional expectation expansion
nodes.statement: \mathbb{E}_f[g(X_\tau) \mid X_0 = x] = (P_\tau g)(x) = \sum_{k \geq 2} e^{-\mu_k \tau}\,\alpha_k\,\psi_k(x).
nodes.label: eq:cond_exp_expansion

nodes.name: SSA spectral formula (derivation)
nodes.statement: S(f) \;=\; \int_0^\infty \rho(\tau)^2\,d\tau \;=\; \sum_{k,\ell \geq 2} w_k w_\ell \int_0^\infty e^{-(\mu_k+\mu_\ell)\tau}\,d\tau \;=\; \sum_{k,\ell \geq 2} \frac{w_k w_\ell}{\mu_k + \mu_\ell},
nodes.label: eq:ST_spectral

nodes.name: Orthogonal Invariance
nodes.statement: Let $C_Y(\tau) = \mathbb{E}[Y_\tau Y_0^\top]$ and $\rho_Y(\tau) = \mathrm{tr} C_Y(\tau)/\mathrm{tr} C_Y(0)$ denote the autocovariance and trace-normalized autocorrelation of the centered process $Y_t$ from Section~\ref{sec:canonical}, and let $C_{QY}(\tau), \rho_{QY}(\tau)$ be the corresponding quantities for the rotated process $QY_t$. For any orthogonal $Q$, $\rho_{QY}(\tau) = \rho_Y(\tau)$.
conclusions: $\rho_{QY}(\tau) = \rho_Y(\tau)$
nodes.statement_short: The trace-normalized autocorrelation is unchanged by rotating the process.
nodes.label: prop:orthogonal_invariance

nodes.name: Proof of orthogonal invariance
nodes.statement: $C_{QY}(\tau) = Q C_Y(\tau) Q^\top$, so $\mathrm{tr}(C_{QY}(\tau)) = \mathrm{tr}(C_Y(\tau))$ by cyclicity. Same at $\tau = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Cyclicity of the trace.

nodes.name: Why trace normalization
nodes.statement: Collapsing the $d \times d$ matrix $C(\tau)$ to a scalar requires a choice. A natural requirement is \emph{basis independence}: the score should not change under an orthogonal coordinate rotation. Using a single coordinate's autocorrelation fails this, since the score depends on which axis is picked. Two basis-independent choices remain: the trace $\mathrm{tr} C(\tau) = \sum_i \lambda_i(\tau)$ and the Frobenius norm $\|C(\tau)\|_F = \sqrt{\sum_i \lambda_i(\tau)^2}$. At first glance Frobenius is appealing because it emphasizes the directions with the largest $C(\tau)$-eigenvalues, which seems to reward barrier structure. But this conflates two distinct properties: by Lemma~\ref{lem:spectral}, $C(\tau)$ is a sum of rank-one components with amplitudes $e^{-\mu_k \tau} \|\alpha_k\|^2$, mixing how slow a mode is ($\mu_k$) with how much variance it carries ($\|\alpha_k\|^2$). The components are not orthogonal in general, so this is not the eigendecomposition of $C(\tau)$, but the Frobenius norm is dominated by whichever rank-one component has the largest current amplitude, which at finite $\tau$ can easily be a fast mode with large amplitude rather than a slow mode. The trace instead aggregates modes linearly, and persistence over $\tau$ is handled by integrating $\rho(\tau)^2$ over time: fast modes decay and drop out of the integrand, slow modes persist, and cross-terms in Equation~\eqref{eq:ST_spectral} reward pairs of simultaneously slow modes. Directional emphasis of slow modes is a separate task, handled by DA (Section~\ref{sec:da}) via eigendecomposition of $C(\tau)$ at large $\tau$, where the exponential weighting has already suppressed fast modes. Dividing by $\mathrm{tr} C(0)$ additionally removes absolute-scale dependence, giving $\rho(\tau) = \mathrm{tr} C(\tau) / \mathrm{tr} C(0)$, which is invariant under orthogonal coordinate changes (Proposition~\ref{prop:orthogonal_invariance}) and under isotropic rescaling of the data.
nodes.statement_short: Trace (not Frobenius) aggregates modes linearly so slow modes persist in the integral; normalizing by tr C(0) removes scale.

nodes.name: Why center by the population mean
nodes.statement: The autocovariance $C(\tau) = \mathbb{E}_f[Y_\tau Y_0^\top]$ requires centering the process, and there are two natural choices: the population mean $\bar x_f = \mathbb{E}_f[X]$, computed once from the stationary distribution, or a per-trajectory mean $\bar{X}^{(n)} = \frac{1}{T+1}\sum_t X_t^{(n)}$. For ergodic processes observed over long horizons these coincide, but for the metastable regime SSA is designed to detect, they differ in a way that matters. When barriers are impassable within $T$, a trajectory initialized in mode $A$ stays in mode $A$ for the entire horizon, and its per-trajectory mean is close to $\mu_A$ rather than $\bar x_f$. Subtracting $\bar{X}^{(n)}$ from such a trajectory zeros out precisely the inter-mode component of interest, producing $\hat\rho(\tau) \approx 0$ for any metastable target. Centering by $\bar x_f$ instead preserves the signal: a trajectory trapped near $\mu_A$ contributes $(\mu_A - \bar x_f)(\mu_A - \bar x_f)^\top$ to $\hat{C}(\tau)$ at every lag, registering as persistent autocorrelation, which is the correct behavior for a metastability measure.
nodes.section: B.3 Why Center by the Population Mean
nodes.statement_short: Per-trajectory centering erases the inter-mode signal of trapped trajectories; population centering keeps it.

nodes.name: Why squaring the autocorrelation
nodes.statement: Without squaring, the integrated autocorrelation \[ \int_0^T \rho(\tau)\,d\tau = \sum_{k \geq 2} w_k \,\frac{1 - e^{-\mu_k T}}{\mu_k} \] is (up to the $1/T$ prefactor) the integrated autocorrelation time $\tau_{\mathrm{cor}}$, a standard mixing measure in MCMC and time-series analysis~\cite{sokal1997,geyer1992}. It is a weighted sum of individual mode contributions. At large $T$ each term saturates at $w_k / \mu_k$, so the sum is dominated by the single smallest eigenvalue: a distribution with one slow barrier and a distribution with five slow barriers score nearly identically provided they share the same $\mu_2$. Squaring before integrating yields cross-terms: \[ S(T) = \sum_{k,\ell \geq 2} w_k w_\ell\, \frac{1 - e^{-(\mu_k + \mu_\ell)T}}{\mu_k + \mu_\ell}. \] The cross-term between modes $k$ and $\ell$ saturates at $w_k w_\ell / (\mu_k + \mu_\ell)$, which is large only when \emph{both} eigenvalues are small. For example, if $\mu_2 = 0.001$ and we compare $\mu_3 = 0.002$ (two slow barriers) against $\mu_3 = 1.0$ (one slow, one fast), the $(k,\ell) = (2,3)$ cross-term contributes $w_2 w_3 / 0.003$ in the first case versus $w_2 w_3 / 1.001$ in the second, a ratio of over $300\times$. The squared formulation thus rewards distributions whose metastable structure involves multiple slow barriers rather than a single dominant one.
nodes.statement_short: Integrating $\rho$ gives an autocorrelation time dominated by $\mu_2$; squaring adds cross-terms that reward several slow barriers.

nodes.name: Monotonicity and Saturation of the spectral kernel
nodes.statement: For any fixed $T > 0$, $h(x) = (1 - e^{-xT})/x$ is strictly decreasing for $x > 0$, with $\lim_{x \to 0^+} h(x) = T$.
nodes.section: B.5 Spectral Kernel: Monotonicity and Saturation
conclusions: strictly decreasing for $x > 0$
$\lim_{x \to 0^+} h(x) = T$
nodes.label: prop:monotonicity

nodes.name: Proof of kernel monotonicity
nodes.statement: L'H\^opital gives the limit. For monotonicity, let $z = xT > 0$. Then $h'(x)$ has the sign of $e^{-z}(z+1) - 1 < 0$ since $e^z > 1+z$ for $z > 0$.
nodes.section: B.5 Spectral Kernel: Monotonicity and Saturation
nodes.statement_short: L'Hopital for the limit; sign of $h'$ via $e^z>1+z$.

nodes.name: Metastable Variance Penalty
nodes.statement: Fix $T > 0$ and weights $\{w_k\}$. Partition the modes $k \geq 2$ into slow and fast, $\mathcal{K}_{\text{slow}}$ and $\mathcal{K}_{\text{fast}}$. As $\mu_k \to 0$ for all $k \in \mathcal{K}_{\text{slow}}$, with $\mu_k$ for $k \in \mathcal{K}_{\text{fast}}$ held fixed, \[ S_T(f) \;=\; T\Big(\textstyle\sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}_{\text{slow}}} w_k\Big)^2 \;+\; O(1). \]
nodes.section: B.5 Spectral Kernel: Monotonicity and Saturation
assumptions: As $\mu_k \to 0$ for all $k \in \mathcal{K}_{\text{slow}}$, with $\mu_k$ for $k \in \mathcal{K}_{\text{fast}}$ held fixed
conclusions: S_T(f) \;=\; T\Big(\textstyle\sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}_{\text{slow}}} w_k\Big)^2 \;+\; O(1)
nodes.statement_short: As slow eigenvalues vanish, $S_T \approx T\,(\text{slow weight})^2$.
nodes.label: cor:metastable_variance

nodes.name: Proof of the metastable variance penalty
nodes.statement: Partition the double sum in~\eqref{eq:ST_spectral} into three blocks by whether each index is slow or fast: \[ S_T(f) = \underbrace{\sum_{k,\ell \in \mathcal{K}_{\text{slow}}}\!\!\! w_k w_\ell\, h(\mu_k+\mu_\ell)}_{A} + \underbrace{2\!\!\sum_{\substack{k \in \mathcal{K}_{\text{slow}} \\ \ell \in \mathcal{K}_{\text{fast}}}}\!\!\! w_k w_\ell\, h(\mu_k+\mu_\ell)}_{B} + \underbrace{\sum_{k,\ell \in \mathcal{K}_{\text{fast}}}\!\!\! w_k w_\ell\, h(\mu_k+\mu_\ell)}_{C}, \] where $h(x) = (1-e^{-xT})/x$. For $(k,\ell) \in \mathcal{K}_{\text{slow}}^2$, $\mu_k + \mu_\ell \to 0$ and $h(\mu_k+\mu_\ell) \to T$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:monotonicity}, so $A \to T \sum_{k,\ell \in \mathcal{K}_{\text{slow}}} w_k w_\ell = T\big(\sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}_{\text{slow}}} w_k\big)^2$. For $B$ and $C$, at least one index is fast. Since $h$ is decreasing and $h(x) \leq 1/x$, each term is bounded by $w_k w_\ell / \mu_\ell$ (for $\ell$ fast), giving $B, C = O(1)$. Hence $S_T(f) = T\big(\sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}_{\text{slow}}} w_k\big)^2 + O(1)$ in the stated limit.
nodes.section: B.5 Spectral Kernel: Monotonicity and Saturation
nodes.statement_short: Split the double sum into slow-slow, slow-fast and fast-fast blocks; the kernel limit gives T on the first, $h\le 1/x$ bounds the rest.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2 (SSA monotonicity)
nodes.statement: For the infinite-horizon score $S(f) = \sum_{i, j \geq 2} w_i w_j / (\mu_i + \mu_j)$, fix $k$. Terms not involving $k$ are independent of $\mu_k$. For off-diagonal terms ($i = k, j \neq k$ or $i \neq k, j = k$), \[ \frac{\partial}{\partial \mu_k} \frac{w_i w_j}{\mu_i + \mu_j} \;=\; -\frac{w_i w_j}{(\mu_i + \mu_j)^2} \;\leq\; 0. \] For the diagonal term $i = j = k$, \[ \frac{\partial}{\partial \mu_k} \frac{w_k^2}{2\mu_k} \;=\; -\frac{w_k^2}{2\mu_k^2} \;\leq\; 0. \] All terms are nonpositive, so the sum is nonincreasing in $\mu_k$, and strictly decreasing whenever $w_k > 0$ (the diagonal term then has strict negative derivative). The same argument applies to the finite-horizon score $S_T(f)$ via Lemma~\ref{lem:spectral}(iii) and the strict monotonicity of the kernel $h_T(x) = (1 - e^{-xT})/x$ in $x > 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate the spectral formula term by term: every derivative is nonpositive, the diagonal one strictly.

nodes.name: Canonical diffusion of a Gaussian is Ornstein-Uhlenbeck
nodes.statement: For $f = \mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma)$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d$ and scalar variance $\sigma_f^2 = \frac{1}{d}\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma)$, the canonical diffusion is Ornstein--Uhlenbeck: \[ dX_t = -\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma_f^2\,\Sigma^{-1} X_t\,dt + \sigma_f\,dW_t, \] with stationary autocovariance $C(\tau) = e^{-\frac{\sigma_f^2}{2}\Sigma^{-1}\tau}\,\Sigma$ and trace-normalized autocorrelation \[ \rho(t) = \frac{\sum_i \lambda_i\, e^{-\sigma_f^2 t/(2\lambda_i)}}{\sum_i \lambda_i}. \]
nodes.section: B.7 Autocovariance Spectrum and SSA Baseline
conclusions: the canonical diffusion is Ornstein--Uhlenbeck
stationary autocovariance $C(\tau) = e^{-\frac{\sigma_f^2}{2}\Sigma^{-1}\tau}\,\Sigma$
nodes.statement_short: For a Gaussian target the canonical diffusion is OU with $C(\tau)=e^{-\sigma_f^2\Sigma^{-1}\tau/2}\Sigma$.

nodes.name: Derivation of the isotropic Gaussian SSA baseline
nodes.statement: For the isotropic case $\Sigma = \sigma^2 I_d$, the canonical diffusion reduces to the standard OU process \[ dX_t = -\tfrac{1}{2} X_t\,dt + \sigma\,dW_t. \] The drift $-\tfrac{1}{2} X_t$ is independent of $\sigma$ because the two factors of $\sigma^2$ cancel: the score is $\nabla \log f(x) = -x/\sigma^2$, and multiplying by the diffusion coefficient $\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2$ leaves just $-\tfrac{1}{2} x$. The noise term $\sigma\,dW_t$ retains the $\sigma$ dependence, so rescaling the data rescales the trajectories without changing the shape of the dynamics, as expected from similarity invariance (Proposition~\ref{prop:similarity_invariance}). The conditional distribution at lag $\tau$ is: \[ X_\tau \mid X_0 \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(e^{-\tau/2}X_0,\;\sigma^2(1 - e^{-\tau})I_d\right). \] The stationary autocovariance is therefore: \[ C(\tau) = \mathbb{E}_f[X_\tau X_0^\top] = e^{-\tau/2}\,\mathbb{E}_f[X_0 X_0^\top] = e^{-\tau/2}\,\sigma^2 I_d. \] That is, $C(\tau)$ is a scalar multiple of the identity at every lag, with the scalar decaying as $e^{-\tau/2}$. All $d$ eigenvalues of $C(\tau)$ are equal to $e^{-\tau/2}\sigma^2$ and decay uniformly to zero. There are no preferred directions at any lag: the isotropic Gaussian has no metastable structure, and DA applied to the population autocovariance would find no distinguished direction. Crucially, the decay rate $e^{-\tau/2}$ is independent of $\sigma^2$. This is a direct consequence of the scalar variance normalization: rescaling the data changes both the drift and diffusion strengths proportionally, leaving the autocorrelation structure invariant.
nodes.section: B.7 Autocovariance Spectrum and SSA Baseline
nodes.statement_short: Isotropic OU: drift $-x/2$, conditional law at lag $\tau$, so $C(\tau)=e^{-\tau/2}\sigma^2 I_d$.

nodes.name: SSA baseline of the isotropic Gaussian equals one
nodes.statement: The trace-normalized autocorrelation is $\rho(\tau) = e^{-\tau/2}$ and $\rho(\tau)^2 = e^{-\tau}$, giving: \[ S_T(f) = \int_0^T e^{-\tau}\,d\tau = 1 - e^{-T} \;\to\; 1 \quad\text{as } T \to \infty. \]
nodes.section: B.7 Autocovariance Spectrum and SSA Baseline
conclusions: S_T(f) = \int_0^T e^{-\tau}\,d\tau = 1 - e^{-T} \;\to\; 1 \quad\text{as } T \to \infty
nodes.statement_short: For an isotropic Gaussian $\rho(\tau)=e^{-\tau/2}$ and SSA $=1$.

nodes.name: Unimodal versus multimodal SSA contrast
nodes.statement: This confirms that SSA introduces no spurious slow timescales for unimodal targets. In contrast, multimodal targets have generator eigenvalues $\mu_k$ exponentially small in the barrier height. By the spectral formula of Corollary~\ref{thm:ssa_spectral}, $S(f) = \sum_{k,\ell \geq 2} w_k w_\ell / (\mu_k + \mu_\ell)$, so each slow-mode pair contributes $w_k w_\ell / (\mu_k + \mu_\ell)$, which diverges as the corresponding barriers grow (i.e., as $\mu_k, \mu_\ell \to 0$). The contrast with the isotropic baseline $S = 1$ is therefore unbounded: SSA grows without limit as barriers deepen, while the unimodal value stays fixed at unity.

nodes.label: eq:rho_clt

nodes.name: Distribution-free 1/N bound on the null variance of rho-hat
nodes.statement: The asymptotic distribution \eqref{eq:rho_clt} provides a null-variance scale for $\hat\rho(\tau)$. Since $d_{\mathrm{eff}} \geq 1$ for any $\Sigma_f$, the universal upper bound $\mathrm{Var}[\hat\rho(\tau)] \leq 1/N$ holds without structural assumptions on $f$, giving the distribution-free signal-above-variance rule \begin{equation} T_{\max} \;=\; \max\!\left\{\tau \,:\, \hat\rho(\tau)^2 \;>\; \frac{1}{N}\right\}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: B.8 Variance-Scale Stopping Rule for Lag-$\tau$ Coupling
conclusions: the universal upper bound $\mathrm{Var}[\hat\rho(\tau)] \leq 1/N$ holds without structural assumptions on $f$
nodes.statement_short: Since $d_{eff}\ge1$, the null variance of $\hat\rho$ is at most 1/N for any f, giving the stopping rule.

nodes.name: Operational threshold versus alpha-level test
nodes.statement: This is an operational threshold (squared autocorrelation exceeds one upper-bound null-variance scale), not a formal $\alpha$-level test; for an $\alpha$-level rule one would replace $1/N$ by $z_{1-\alpha/2}^2/(N\,d_{\mathrm{eff}})$ using the plug-in estimate of $d_{\mathrm{eff}}$. Under $H_0$, retaining a lag $\tau$ with $\hat\rho(\tau)^2 > 1/N$ corresponds to a z-score of at least $\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{eff}}}$, conservative on isotropic targets and at the one-standard-deviation scale at $d_{\mathrm{eff}} = 1$. A sharper data-adaptive threshold replaces $1/N$ with the plug-in estimate $\mathrm{tr}(\hat C(0)^2)/(N\,\mathrm{tr}(\hat C(0))^2)$ from \eqref{eq:rho_clt}, computable from the same $\hat C(0)$ already needed for normalization.
nodes.section: B.8 Variance-Scale Stopping Rule for Lag-$\tau$ Coupling
nodes.statement_short: The 1/N rule is a variance-scale threshold, not an $\alpha$-level test; sharper plug-in thresholds use $d_{eff}$.

nodes.name: Scope of the trace CLT versus the DA noise floor
nodes.statement: The CLT \eqref{eq:rho_clt} holds for any fixed $d$ as $N \to \infty$ and assumes only finite second moments of $f$; it applies specifically to the trace functional $\mathrm{tr} \hat C(\tau)$ that SSA integrates. This is a distinct regime from the DA noise floor of Theorem~\ref{thm:limit-spectrum}, which is derived in the proportional limit $d/N \to \gamma \in (0, \infty)$ and characterizes the top eigenvalue of $\hat C(\tau)$ rather than its trace. The two thresholds are not interchangeable: \eqref{eq:rho_clt_threshold} averages over $d$ directions and is the right object for SSA's scalar readout, while $\lambda_+(\tau)$ takes the maximum over directions and is the right object for DA's eigendecomposition.
