conclusions: The leading DA direction therefore converges to the inter-mode direction $\mu_A - \mu_B$ for any $A_0$ in this regime.

nodes.name: Underdamped Langevin dynamics
nodes.statement: Real physical systems (proteins, peptides, biomolecules in solvent) are governed not by the canonical overdamped diffusion but by underdamped Langevin dynamics on phase space $(q, p) \in \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d$: \begin{equation} dq_t \;=\; M^{-1} p_t\,dt, \qquad dp_t \;=\; -\nabla U(q_t)\,dt \;-\; \eta\,M^{-1} p_t\,dt \;+\; \sqrt{2 \eta \beta^{-1}}\,dW_t, \end{equation} with mass matrix $M \succ 0$, friction $\eta > 0$, inverse temperature $\beta = 1/k_B T$, and potential $U(q) = -\beta^{-1}\log f(q)$.

nodes.name: Underdamped Langevin SDE
nodes.statement: dq_t \;=\; M^{-1} p_t\,dt, \qquad dp_t \;=\; -\nabla U(q_t)\,dt \;-\; \eta\,M^{-1} p_t\,dt \;+\; \sqrt{2 \eta \beta^{-1}}\,dW_t,
nodes.label: eq:underdamped

nodes.name: Slow relaxation rates mu^UD and mu^OD
nodes.statement: We write $\mu_k^{\rm UD}(\eta, \beta)$ for its slow real relaxation rates in the metastable asymptotic regime considered below, and $\mu_k^{\rm OD}(f)$ for those of the overdamped canonical diffusion attached to $f$.

nodes.name: Smoluchowski limit
nodes.statement: As $\eta \to \infty$, the time-rescaled position trajectory $q_{\eta t}$ of the underdamped Langevin equation~\eqref{eq:underdamped} converges weakly to an overdamped Langevin diffusion with stationary marginal $f$ and a constant diffusion matrix determined by $M$ and $\beta$. Its slow eigenvalues are the overdamped rates of that limiting diffusion; by Appendix~\ref{app:robustness} (Proposition~\ref{prop:robustness_ito}), they share the same metastable barrier exponents as the canonical scalar-diffusion rates $\mu_k^{\rm OD}(f)$.
conclusions: the time-rescaled position trajectory $q_{\eta t}$ of the underdamped Langevin equation~\eqref{eq:underdamped} converges weakly to an overdamped Langevin diffusion with stationary marginal $f$ and a constant diffusion matrix determined by $M$ and $\beta$
nodes.statement_short: High-friction underdamped Langevin converges to an overdamped diffusion sharing the canonical diffusion's barrier exponents.
nodes.label: thm:smoluchowski

nodes.name: Eyring-Kramers asymptotics
nodes.statement: Standard Eyring--Kramers theory~\cite{kramers1940,bovier_dh2015,nelson1967} for a metastable density $f$ with a finite collection of well-separated basins (well-defined saddle structure, non-degenerate quadratic minima and saddles) gives slow rates of the underdamped Langevin generator at fixed positive $\eta$ and $M$ of the form \[ \mu_k^{\rm UD}(\eta, \beta;\, f) \;\sim\; \kappa_k(\eta, M;\, f)\,\exp\!\bigl(-\beta\,\Delta U_k(f)\bigr) \quad \text{as } \beta \to \infty, \] with $\kappa_k > 0$ depending on $\eta, M$ and local curvatures, and $\Delta U_k(f)$ a barrier height determined by $f$ alone. The same form holds for the overdamped rates $\mu_k^{\rm OD}$ with a different prefactor.
assumptions: a metastable density $f$ with a finite collection of well-separated basins (well-defined saddle structure, non-degenerate quadratic minima and saddles)
conclusions: \mu_k^{\rm UD}(\eta, \beta;\, f) \;\sim\; \kappa_k(\eta, M;\, f)\,\exp\!\bigl(-\beta\,\Delta U_k(f)\bigr) \quad \text{as } \beta \to \infty
The same form holds for the overdamped rates $\mu_k^{\rm OD}$ with a different prefactor.
nodes.statement_short: Slow rates are a prefactor times $\exp(-\beta\Delta U_k)$ with barrier heights fixed by f.

nodes.name: Asymptotic ordering implication for kinetic dynamics
nodes.statement: For two densities $f_A, f_B$ with non-degenerate barrier-height ordering at index $k$, the Eyring--Kramers form implies that in the deep-barrier limit $\beta\,|\Delta U_k(f_A) - \Delta U_k(f_B)| \to \infty$ (at fixed $\eta, M$), the sign of $\mu_k^{\rm UD}(f_A) - \mu_k^{\rm UD}(f_B)$ is determined by the barrier-height comparison and matches the corresponding overdamped sign.
assumptions: two densities $f_A, f_B$ with non-degenerate barrier-height ordering at index $k$
in the deep-barrier limit $\beta\,|\Delta U_k(f_A) - \Delta U_k(f_B)| \to \infty$ (at fixed $\eta, M$)
conclusions: the sign of $\mu_k^{\rm UD}(f_A) - \mu_k^{\rm UD}(f_B)$ is determined by the barrier-height comparison and matches the corresponding overdamped sign
nodes.statement_short: In the deep-barrier limit underdamped and overdamped dynamics order slow rates the same way.

nodes.name: Derivation sketch of the kinetic ordering implication
nodes.statement: The Eyring--Kramers form gives $\mu_k^{\rm UD}(\eta, \beta;\, f) \sim \kappa_k(\eta, M;\, f)\exp(-\beta \Delta U_k(f))$ as $\beta \to \infty$. Taking the ratio of the rates for $f_A$ and $f_B$, the prefactor ratio is finite and positive while the exponent diverges (in absolute value) as $\beta \to \infty$, so the sign of $\mu_k^{\rm UD}(f_A) - \mu_k^{\rm UD}(f_B)$ is determined by $\Delta U_k(f_B) - \Delta U_k(f_A)$ in the deep-barrier limit. The same applies to $\mu_k^{\rm OD}$ via the Smoluchowski limit.
nodes.statement_short: Ratio of Eyring-Kramers rates: finite prefactor ratio, diverging exponent.

nodes.name: Consequence for slow-mode orderings
nodes.statement: For \emph{leading exponential escape rates}, the deep-barrier asymptotic predicts that the canonical diffusion and any underdamped Langevin process with the same stationary marginal $f$ have the same slow-CV ordering, since both inherit it from the $f$-determined barrier-height profile. SSA values, DA directions, and prefactors can still differ between the two dynamics outside the asymptotic regime; what is preserved asymptotically is the ordering of the leading exponents. The empirical agreement between DA's static-sample recovery on alanine dipeptide (Section~\ref{sec:exp_molecular}) and TICA's trajectory-based recovery is consistent with this prediction in the regime $\beta \Delta U_k \gg 1$ (alanine dihedrals at 300\,K).

nodes.name: Algorithmic relation of DA to TICA
nodes.statement: DA and TICA differ in the eigenvalue-problem formulation, not merely in the underlying dynamics. DA solves the standard eigenvalue problem $C(\tau)v = \lambda v$, retaining variance weighting and ranking directions by absolute slow-mode contribution to the autocovariance. TICA solves the generalized eigenvalue problem $C(\tau)v = \lambda C(0)v$, normalizing out per-direction variance and ranking directions by relaxation \emph{rate}. Had we adopted the full-covariance convention $A_0 = \mathrm{Cov}_f(X)$ instead of the scalar-variance choice $A_0 = \sigma_f^2 I_d$ (Appendix~\ref{app:diffusion_matrix_choice}), DA and TICA would coincide in that respect. We did not, for two reasons: a conceptual one (the affine-invariant construction has counterintuitive edge cases) and a computational one (DA avoids inverting $\hat C(0)$, which scales better in high dimensions). Systematically exploring the full-covariance variant is a natural direction for future work.
nodes.statement_short: DA solves $C(\tau)v=\lambda v$ (variance-weighted), TICA $C(\tau)v=\lambda C(0)v$; they coincide for $A_0=\mathrm{Cov}_f$.

nodes.name: Non-asymptotic underdamped/overdamped rate comparison
nodes.statement: Without taking limits, comparing $\eta\,\mu_k^{\rm UD}(\eta, \beta)$ to $\mu_k^{\rm OD}(f)$ at finite friction and finite temperature would require a non-asymptotic relative-error statement of the form \[ \Bigl|\,\eta\,\mu_k^{\rm UD}(\eta, \beta;\, f) \,/\, \mu_k^{\rm OD}(f) \;-\; 1\,\Bigr| \;\le\; C_1/\eta^2 \;+\; C_2\,e^{-\beta\,\Delta U_k(f)}. \] A clean version of this bound is plausible by perturbation theory of the underdamped generator on phase space, but is outside the scope of this paper; we leave it to follow-up work.
conclusions: \Bigl|\,\eta\,\mu_k^{\rm UD}(\eta, \beta;\, f) \,/\, \mu_k^{\rm OD}(f) \;-\; 1\,\Bigr| \;\le\; C_1/\eta^2 \;+\; C_2\,e^{-\beta\,\Delta U_k(f)}
nodes.statement_short: A relative-error bound $C_1/\eta^2+C_2e^{-\beta\Delta U_k}$ between scaled underdamped and overdamped rates is plausible but unproven.

nodes.name: Derivation of the Tweedie identity
nodes.statement: A diffusion model defines a forward noising process $q(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}(x_t; \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t} x_0, \sigma_t^2 I)$, where $\sigma_t^2 = 1 - \bar\alpha_t$. The marginal at time $t$ is \[ f_t(x) = \int q(x \mid x_0) f(x_0)\, dx_0. \] Using Bayes' rule to express the posterior $p(x_0 \mid x_t)$, the score of this marginal satisfies \[ \nabla \log f_t(x) = -\frac{x - \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_t = x]}{\sigma_t^2}. \] One can notice that any sample from this kernel can be written in the reparameterized form \[ x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sigma_t\,\epsilon, \qquad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), \] which isolates the structured signal $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0$ from the additive Gaussian noise $\sigma_t\,\epsilon$. Rearranging gives the residual noise explicitly: \[ \epsilon = \frac{x_t - \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0}{\sigma_t}, \qquad \text{equivalently,} \qquad x_0 = \frac{x_t - \sigma_t\,\epsilon}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}}. \] A diffusion model trains a denoiser $\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)$ to predict this noise $\epsilon$, so that $\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_t] \approx (x_t - \sigma_t\,\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t))/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}$. Substituting into the score expression above yields the Tweedie identity: \[ \nabla \log f_t(x) = -\frac{\epsilon_\theta(x, t)}{\sigma_t}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Bayes' rule gives the score through the posterior mean; substituting the denoiser's estimate of $x_0$ yields $-\epsilon_\theta/\sigma_t$.

nodes.name: Recovery of the data score as t to 0
nodes.statement:
As $t 	o 0$, $\sigma_t 	o 0$ and $\sqrt{ ar\alpha_t} 	o 1$, so the forward kernel $q(x_t \mid x_0)$ concentrates: $f_t 	o f$ in distribution. More precisely, for any smooth test function $\phi$, \[ \int \phi(x) f_t(x)\, dx \;	o\; \int \phi(x) f(x)\, dx, \] and under mild regularity on $f$ the scores converge pointwise: $
abla \log f_t(x) 	o 
abla \log f(x)$. Consequently, evaluating the Tweedie identity at a small but finite $t_{\mathrm{small}}$ gives \[ 
abla \log f(x) \approx - rac{\epsilon_	heta(x,\, t_{\mathrm{small}})}{\sigma_{t_{\mathrm{small}}}}, \] with approximation error controlled by $\sigma_{t_{\mathrm{small}}}$ and the smoothness of $f$. This provides a tractable score oracle for the data distribution through a single forward pass of the trained denoiser, with no density estimation step and no dependence on dimensionality. The division by $\sigma_t$ is numerically benign at the first discrete timestep of a standard linear schedule ($\sigma_1 \approx 0.01$).
nodes.section: E.2 Recovery of the Data Score as $t \to 0$
nodes.statement_short: At small noise the Tweedie score approximates $\nabla\log f$ with one denoiser pass.

nodes.name: Iso-Gaussian null via large-t score evaluation
nodes.statement: The same trained denoiser provides a self-contained iso-Gaussian score oracle for the operational noise floor of Algorithm~\ref{alg:operational_floor}. By construction, the noised marginal $f_t$ at large $t$ is close to $\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_t^2 I)$, so the denoiser learns the linear iso-Gaussian score $\nabla \log f_t(x) \approx -x/\sigma_t^2$ at that level. Evaluating the canonical diffusion with this same score network at $t = t_{\mathrm{null}} \gg 0$ therefore runs the iso-Gaussian null through the entire downstream pipeline (sampling, decoding, embedding) at no extra training cost. We use this for the elderly DA experiment in Section~\ref{sec:exp_sdxl} (details in Appendix~\ref{app:sdxl_elderly}).
nodes.section: E.3 Iso-Gaussian Null via Large-$t$ Score Evaluation
nodes.statement_short: At large noise the same denoiser gives the linear iso-Gaussian score, running the null through the full pipeline.

nodes.name: T-stability of fixed-profile SSA rankings
nodes.statement: For comparisons of the fixed-spectral-profile kind covered by Proposition~\ref{prop:ssa_monotonicity} (one density's spectral profile dominates another's term-by-term), $S_A(T) > S_B(T)$ for every $T > 0$, and increasing $T$ can only widen the gap.
assumptions: comparisons of the fixed-spectral-profile kind covered by Proposition~\ref{prop:ssa_monotonicity} (one density's spectral profile dominates another's term-by-term)
conclusions: $S_A(T) > S_B(T)$ for every $T > 0$
increasing $T$ can only widen the gap
also_stated_at: By Proposition~\ref{prop:ssa_monotonicity}, in fixed-spectral-profile comparisons $S(T_{\max})$ is monotone in every $\mu_k$ at every $T_{\max}$: truncation underestimates absolute values but preserves rankings, and faster-mixing competitors only contribute near-zero past their own stopping lag, so the gap between scores can only widen as $T_{\max}$ grows.
nodes.statement_short: If one spectral profile dominates another term by term, its finite-horizon SSA is larger at every horizon, with a widening gap.

nodes.name: Fokker-Planck equation
nodes.statement:
For a general diffusion with $A(x)\equiv A_0$ constant, the Fokker--Planck equation is \[ \partial_t p(x,t) = -
abla \cdot (b(x)\,p(x,t)) +  rac{1}{2}\,
abla \cdot  ig(A_0 
abla p(x,t) ig). \]
nodes.statement_short: Write the Fokker-Planck equation for constant $A_0$.

nodes.name: Probability current
nodes.statement: Define the probability current $J_p(x) := b(x)\,p(x) - \frac{1}{2}A_0 \nabla p(x)$. Stationarity with density $f$ requires $\nabla \cdot J_f(x) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the probability current; stationarity means zero divergence.

nodes.name: Reversibility as zero current
nodes.statement: Reversibility with respect to $f$ is equivalent to the stronger condition $J_f(x)\equiv 0$ (vanishing probability current; standard characterization of reversible diffusions, see~\cite[Ch.~4]{Pavliotis2014}).
nodes.statement_short: Reversibility is equivalent to vanishing current (cited).

nodes.name: Solve for the drift
nodes.statement: With $A(x)\equiv A_0$ and $J_f\equiv 0$, we have $0 = b(x)f(x) - \frac{1}{2}A_0\nabla f(x)$, so $b(x) = \frac{1}{2}A_0 \nabla \log f(x)$, which uniquely determines the drift and hence the diffusion.
nodes.statement_short: Zero current solves to $b=\tfrac12A_0\nabla\log f$.

nodes.name: Density of Y
nodes.statement: Let $Y = cQX + b$. By change of variables, $Y$ has density \[ f_Y(y) = c^{-d} f\!\left(c^{-1} Q^\top (y - b)\right). \]
nodes.statement_short: Change of variables for the density of $Y$.

nodes.name: Ito's lemma
nodes.statement: Applying It\^o's lemma to $Y_t = cQX_t + b$ yields \[ dY_t = \tfrac{1}{2} c \sigma_f^2\, Q \nabla_x \log f(X_t)\,dt + c \sigma_f\, Q\,dW_t. \]
nodes.statement_short: Apply Ito's lemma to the affine map.

nodes.name: Transform variance and score
nodes.statement:
The scalar variance of $Y$ is $\sigma_Y^2 = c^2 \sigma_f^2$, and the score transforms as $
abla_y \log f_Y(y) =  rac{1}{c} Q 
abla_x \log f(x)$. Substituting gives \[ dY_t = 	frac{1}{2} \sigma_Y^2\, 
abla \log f_Y(Y_t)\,dt + \sigma_Y\,d	ilde{W}_t, \] where $	ilde{W}_t = Q W_t$ is again standard Brownian motion (orthogonal transformations preserve the distribution of $W$). This is exactly the canonical diffusion for $f_Y$.
nodes.statement_short: Substitute the transformed variance and score: canonical SDE for $f_Y$.

nodes.name: Unitary intertwining
nodes.statement: The change-of-variables map $U\varphi(y) := \varphi(c^{-1}Q^\top(y - b))$ is unitary $L^2(f\,dx) \to L^2(f_Y\,dy)$ (the density Jacobian $f_Y(y)\,dy = f(x)\,dx$ makes $U$ an isometry without further normalization), and intertwines the two generators: $\mathcal{L}_{f_Y} U = U \mathcal{L}_f$. Hence the spectra coincide.
nodes.statement_short: A unitary map intertwines the generators, so spectra agree.

nodes.name: Eigen-expansion of coordinates
nodes.statement: Let $P_\tau = e^{\tau\mathcal{L}_f}$ denote the Markov semigroup generated by $\mathcal{L}_f$. By the Kolmogorov backward equation, $P_\tau$ acts as conditional expectation: $\mathbb{E}_f[\varphi(X_\tau) \mid X_0 = x] = (P_\tau \varphi)(x)$ for any $\varphi \in L^2(f\,dx)$. By the spectral theorem for self-adjoint operators, $\{\psi_k\}_{k \geq 1}$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $L^2(f\,dx)$ and $P_\tau \psi_k = e^{-\mu_k \tau}\psi_k$. The centered coordinate map $g(x) := x - \bar x_f$ is vector-valued; we assume $f$ has finite second moments so that each component $g_j \in L^2(f\,dx)$. Expanding each component in the eigenbasis, \[ g_j(x) = \sum_{k \geq 1} (\alpha_k)_j\, \psi_k(x), \qquad (\alpha_k)_j = \langle g_j, \psi_k\rangle_f = \int (x_j - (\bar x_f)_j)\,\psi_k(x)\,f(x)\,dx. \] Stacking across coordinates gives $g(x) = \sum_{k \geq 1} \alpha_k\,\psi_k(x)$. The $k = 1$ term drops out because $\psi_1 \equiv 1$, so $(\alpha_1)_j = \mathbb{E}_f[X_j] - (\bar x_f)_j = 0$ by the definition of $\bar x_f$. Hence $g = \sum_{k \geq 2}\alpha_k\,\psi_k$ and, applying $P_\tau$ coordinate-wise, \begin{equation} \mathbb{E}_f[g(X_\tau) \mid X_0 = x] = (P_\tau g)(x) = \sum_{k \geq 2} e^{-\mu_k \tau}\,\alpha_k\,\psi_k(x). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Expand centered coordinates in the eigenbasis and apply the semigroup.

nodes.name: Part (i): autocovariance
nodes.statement: \textit{(i)} Writing the expectation over the joint stationary distribution of $(X_0, X_\tau)$ and integrating out $X_\tau$ first via the tower property, \[ C(\tau) = \mathbb{E}_f[Y_\tau Y_0^\top] = \int \mathbb{E}_f[Y_\tau \mid X_0 = x]\,(x - \bar x_f)^\top\, f(x)\,dx. \] Substituting~\eqref{eq:cond_exp_expansion} and pulling the sum outside the integral, \[ C(\tau) = \sum_{k \geq 2} e^{-\mu_k \tau}\,\alpha_k \left[\int \psi_k(x)\,(x - \bar x_f)^\top f(x)\,dx\right]. \] The bracketed quantity is a row vector whose $j$-th entry is $\int (x_j - (\bar x_f)_j)\,\psi_k(x)\,f(x)\,dx = (\alpha_k)_j$, i.e., it equals $\alpha_k^\top$. Therefore \[ C(\tau) = \sum_{k \geq 2} e^{-\mu_k \tau}\,\alpha_k\,\alpha_k^\top. \]
nodes.statement_short: Tower property and the expansion give $C(\tau)$.

nodes.name: Part (ii): autocorrelation
nodes.statement: \textit{(ii)} Taking the trace of (i) and using $\mathrm{tr}(\alpha_k \alpha_k^\top) = \|\alpha_k\|^2$, \[ \mathrm{tr} C(\tau) = \sum_{k \geq 2} e^{-\mu_k \tau}\,\|\alpha_k\|^2. \] At $\tau = 0$, $\mathrm{tr} C(0) = \sum_{k \geq 2}\|\alpha_k\|^2$, so \[ \rho(\tau) = \frac{\mathrm{tr} C(\tau)}{\mathrm{tr} C(0)} = \sum_{k \geq 2} e^{-\mu_k \tau}\,w_k, \qquad w_k := \frac{\|\alpha_k\|^2}{\sum_{j \geq 2}\|\alpha_j\|^2}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Trace and normalize to get $\rho(\tau)$.

nodes.name: Part (iii): spectral formula
nodes.statement: \textit{(iii) Spectral formula for SSA (Corollary~\ref{thm:ssa_spectral}).} From (ii), $\rho(\tau)^2 = \sum_{k, \ell \geq 2} w_k w_\ell\, e^{-(\mu_k + \mu_\ell)\tau}$. Integrating term-by-term over $[0, \infty)$, \begin{equation} S(f) \;=\; \int_0^\infty \rho(\tau)^2\,d\tau \;=\; \sum_{k,\ell \geq 2} w_k w_\ell \int_0^\infty e^{-(\mu_k+\mu_\ell)\tau}\,d\tau \;=\; \sum_{k,\ell \geq 2} \frac{w_k w_\ell}{\mu_k + \mu_\ell}, \end{equation} which is the spectral formula of Corollary~\ref{thm:ssa_spectral}.
nodes.statement_short: Square and integrate term by term.

nodes.name: Partition into blocks
nodes.statement: Partition the double sum in~\eqref{eq:ST_spectral} into three blocks by whether each index is slow or fast: \[ S_T(f) = \underbrace{\sum_{k,\ell \in \mathcal{K}_{\text{slow}}}\!\!\! w_k w_\ell\, h(\mu_k+\mu_\ell)}_{A} + \underbrace{2\!\!\sum_{\substack{k \in \mathcal{K}_{\text{slow}} \\ \ell \in \mathcal{K}_{\text{fast}}}}\!\!\! w_k w_\ell\, h(\mu_k+\mu_\ell)}_{B} + \underbrace{\sum_{k,\ell \in \mathcal{K}_{\text{fast}}}\!\!\! w_k w_\ell\, h(\mu_k+\mu_\ell)}_{C}, \] where $h(x) = (1-e^{-xT})/x$.
nodes.statement_short: Split the double sum into slow-slow, slow-fast, fast-fast blocks.
nodes.section: B.5 Spectral Kernel: Monotonicity and Saturation

nodes.name: Slow block limit
nodes.statement: For $(k,\ell) \in \mathcal{K}_{\text{slow}}^2$, $\mu_k + \mu_\ell \to 0$ and $h(\mu_k+\mu_\ell) \to T$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:monotonicity}, so $A \to T \sum_{k,\ell \in \mathcal{K}_{\text{slow}}} w_k w_\ell = T\big(\sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}_{\text{slow}}} w_k\big)^2$.
nodes.statement_short: The kernel limit $h\to T$ gives the slow block.
nodes.section: B.5 Spectral Kernel: Monotonicity and Saturation

nodes.name: Fast blocks bounded
nodes.statement: For $B$ and $C$, at least one index is fast. Since $h$ is decreasing and $h(x) \leq 1/x$, each term is bounded by $w_k w_\ell / \mu_\ell$ (for $\ell$ fast), giving $B, C = O(1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the other blocks by $h(x)\le1/x$.
nodes.section: B.5 Spectral Kernel: Monotonicity and Saturation

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence $S_T(f) = T\big(\sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}_{\text{slow}}} w_k\big)^2 + O(1)$ in the stated limit.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the blocks.
nodes.section: B.5 Spectral Kernel: Monotonicity and Saturation

nodes.name: Fix an index
nodes.statement: For the infinite-horizon score $S(f) = \sum_{i, j \geq 2} w_i w_j / (\mu_i + \mu_j)$, fix $k$. Terms not involving $k$ are independent of $\mu_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix k; only terms with k depend on $\mu_k$.

nodes.name: Off-diagonal derivatives
nodes.statement: For off-diagonal terms ($i = k, j \neq k$ or $i \neq k, j = k$), \[ \frac{\partial}{\partial \mu_k} \frac{w_i w_j}{\mu_i + \mu_j} \;=\; -\frac{w_i w_j}{(\mu_i + \mu_j)^2} \;\leq\; 0. \]
nodes.statement_short: Off-diagonal derivatives are nonpositive.

nodes.name: Diagonal derivative
nodes.statement: For the diagonal term $i = j = k$, \[ \frac{\partial}{\partial \mu_k} \frac{w_k^2}{2\mu_k} \;=\; -\frac{w_k^2}{2\mu_k^2} \;\leq\; 0. \]
nodes.statement_short: The diagonal derivative is nonpositive.

nodes.name: Monotonicity of S
nodes.statement: All terms are nonpositive, so the sum is nonincreasing in $\mu_k$, and strictly decreasing whenever $w_k > 0$ (the diagonal term then has strict negative derivative).
nodes.statement_short: Sum of nonpositive derivatives; strict when $w_k>0$.

nodes.name: Finite horizon
nodes.statement: The same argument applies to the finite-horizon score $S_T(f)$ via Lemma~\ref{lem:spectral}(iii) and the strict monotonicity of the kernel $h_T(x) = (1 - e^{-xT})/x$ in $x > 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat with the strictly decreasing kernel $h_T$.

nodes.name: Isotropic OU process
nodes.statement: For the isotropic case $\Sigma = \sigma^2 I_d$, the canonical diffusion reduces to the standard OU process \[ dX_t = -\tfrac{1}{2} X_t\,dt + \sigma\,dW_t. \] The drift $-\tfrac{1}{2} X_t$ is independent of $\sigma$ because the two factors of $\sigma^2$ cancel: the score is $\nabla \log f(x) = -x/\sigma^2$, and multiplying by the diffusion coefficient $\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2$ leaves just $-\tfrac{1}{2} x$. The noise term $\sigma\,dW_t$ retains the $\sigma$ dependence, so rescaling the data rescales the trajectories without changing the shape of the dynamics, as expected from similarity invariance (Proposition~\ref{prop:similarity_invariance}).
nodes.statement_short: Specialize to the isotropic OU process with drift $-x/2$.
nodes.section: B.7 Autocovariance Spectrum and SSA Baseline

nodes.name: Autocovariance is scalar
nodes.statement: The conditional distribution at lag $\tau$ is: \[ X_\tau \mid X_0 \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(e^{-\tau/2}X_0,\;\sigma^2(1 - e^{-\tau})I_d\right). \] The stationary autocovariance is therefore: \[ C(\tau) = \mathbb{E}_f[X_\tau X_0^\top] = e^{-\tau/2}\,\mathbb{E}_f[X_0 X_0^\top] = e^{-\tau/2}\,\sigma^2 I_d. \] That is, $C(\tau)$ is a scalar multiple of the identity at every lag, with the scalar decaying as $e^{-\tau/2}$. All $d$ eigenvalues of $C(\tau)$ are equal to $e^{-\tau/2}\sigma^2$ and decay uniformly to zero. There are no preferred directions at any lag: the isotropic Gaussian has no metastable structure, and DA applied to the population autocovariance would find no distinguished direction.
nodes.statement_short: Conditional law gives $C(\tau)=e^{-\tau/2}\sigma^2I_d$.
nodes.section: B.7 Autocovariance Spectrum and SSA Baseline

nodes.name: Scale independence
nodes.statement: Crucially, the decay rate $e^{-\tau/2}$ is independent of $\sigma^2$. This is a direct consequence of the scalar variance normalization: rescaling the data changes both the drift and diffusion strengths proportionally, leaving the autocorrelation structure invariant.
nodes.statement_short: The decay rate does not depend on $\sigma^2$.
nodes.section: B.7 Autocovariance Spectrum and SSA Baseline

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: Write $Y_n = X_0^{(n)} - \bar x_f$ and $Y_n' = X_\tau^{(n)} - \bar x_f$. Under $H_0$, $Y_n$ and $Y_n'$ are independent draws from the centered version of $f$; in particular, $\mathbb{E}[Y_n] = \mathbb{E}[Y_n'] = 0$ and $\mathbb{E}[Y_n Y_n^\top] = \mathbb{E}[Y_n' Y_n'^\top] = \Sigma_f := \mathrm{Cov}_f(X)$. The trace-normalized autocorrelation is \[ \hat\rho(\tau) = \frac{\mathrm{tr} \hat C(\tau)}{\mathrm{tr} \hat C(0)} = \frac{A_N}{B_N}, \qquad A_N := \tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N Y_n^\top Y_n', \qquad B_N := \mathrm{tr} \hat C(0). \]
nodes.statement_short: Write $\hat\rho$ as a ratio $A_N/B_N$ of sample means.
nodes.section: B.8 Variance-Scale Stopping Rule for Lag-$\tau$ Coupling

nodes.name: Numerator moments
nodes.statement: Each summand $Z_n := Y_n^\top Y_n' = \mathrm{tr}(Y_n' Y_n^\top)$ satisfies, under $H_0$, $\mathbb{E}[Z_n] = \mathrm{tr}(\mathbb{E}[Y_n' Y_n^\top]) = \mathrm{tr}(\mathbb{E}[Y_n']\mathbb{E}[Y_n]^\top) = 0$ and \[ \mathrm{Var}[Z_n] \;=\; \mathbb{E}[(Y_n^\top Y_n')^2] \;=\; \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{tr}(Y_n Y_n^\top Y_n' Y_n'^\top)] \;=\; \mathrm{tr}(\mathbb{E}[Y_n Y_n^\top]\,\mathbb{E}[Y_n' Y_n'^\top]) \;=\; \mathrm{tr}(\Sigma_f^2), \] using independence of $Y_n, Y_n'$ in the third equality. Hence $\mathbb{E}[A_N] = 0$ and $\mathrm{Var}[A_N] = \mathrm{tr}(\Sigma_f^2)/N$.
nodes.statement_short: Under independence the numerator has mean 0 and variance tr$(\Sigma_f^2)/N$.
nodes.section: B.8 Variance-Scale Stopping Rule for Lag-$\tau$ Coupling

nodes.name: Denominator moments
nodes.statement: The denominator $B_N = \mathrm{tr} \hat C(0) = \tfrac{1}{N}\sum_n \|Y_n\|^2$ is a sample mean of i.i.d.\ scalars. Each summand $W_n := \|Y_n\|^2 = \mathrm{tr}(Y_n Y_n^\top)$ satisfies \[ \mathbb{E}[W_n] = \mathrm{tr}(\mathbb{E}[Y_n Y_n^\top]) = \mathrm{tr}\Sigma_f, \] so $\mathbb{E}[B_N] = \mathrm{tr}\Sigma_f$. Expanding in coordinates, \[ \mathbb{E}[\|Y_n\|^4] = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\Bigl(\sum_i Y_{n,i}^2\Bigr)^2\right] = \sum_{i,j} \mathbb{E}[Y_{n,i}^2 Y_{n,j}^2]. \] For any $f$ with finite fourth moments, the second-moment relations $\mathbb{E}[Y_{n,i}^2 Y_{n,j}^2] = \Sigma_{f,ii}\Sigma_{f,jj} + 2\Sigma_{f,ij}^2 + \kappa_{ij}$, where $\kappa_{ij}$ is the fourth-order cumulant correction at indices $(i,j)$ (zero for Gaussian $f$), yield \[ \mathbb{E}[\|Y_n\|^4] \;=\; \sum_{i,j} \Sigma_{f,ii}\Sigma_{f,jj} + 2\sum_{i,j}\Sigma_{f,ij}^2 + \sum_{i,j}\kappa_{ij} \;=\; (\mathrm{tr}\Sigma_f)^2 + 2\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma_f^2) + \kappa_f, \] with $\kappa_f := \sum_{i,j}\kappa_{ij}$, where $\kappa_f$ collects the fourth-order cumulant contributions of $f$ (vanishing in the Gaussian case). Assuming $f$ has finite fourth moments, $\kappa_f$ is finite, so $\mathrm{Var}[W_n] = 2\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma_f^2) + \kappa_f$ is a finite quantity depending on $\Sigma_f$ and the fourth-order structure of $f$. Averaging over $N$ i.i.d.\ copies, $\mathrm{Var}[B_N] = \mathrm{Var}[W_n]/N$, so $B_N$ concentrates at $\mathrm{tr}\Sigma_f$ at the $1/\sqrt{N}$ rate.
nodes.statement_short: The denominator concentrates at tr$\Sigma_f$.
nodes.section: B.8 Variance-Scale Stopping Rule for Lag-$\tau$ Coupling

nodes.name: CLT and delta method
nodes.statement: The denominator $B_N$ has mean $\mathrm{tr}\Sigma_f$ and variance $O(1/N)$ (previous paragraph), so by the multivariate CLT and the delta method~\cite{vanderVaart1998} applied to the smooth map $g(a, b) = a/b$ at $(0, \mathrm{tr}\Sigma_f)$ (where $\partial_a g = 1/\mathrm{tr}\Sigma_f$ and $\partial_b g = 0$ because $a = 0$): \begin{equation} \sqrt{N}\,\hat\rho(\tau) \;\xrightarrow{d}\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(0,\; \frac{1}{d_{\mathrm{eff}}}\right), \qquad d_{\mathrm{eff}} := \frac{(\mathrm{tr}\Sigma_f)^2}{\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma_f^2)}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Multivariate CLT and delta method at $(0,\mathrm{tr}\Sigma_f)$.
nodes.section: B.8 Variance-Scale Stopping Rule for Lag-$\tau$ Coupling

nodes.name: Asymptotic variance
nodes.statement:
The asymptotic variance is $
abla g^	op \Sigma_T 
abla g$, where $\Sigma_T$ is the covariance of $(Z_n, W_n)$. The diagonal entries are $\mathrm{Var}[Z_n] = \mathrm{tr}(\Sigma_f^2)$ (shown above) and $\mathrm{Var}[W_n] < \infty$. The off-diagonal vanishes under $H_0$: conditioning on $Y_n$, $\mathbb{E}[Z_n W_n] = \mathbb{E}[W_n \cdot \mathbb{E}[Z_n \mid Y_n]] = 0$ since $\mathbb{E}[Z_n \mid Y_n] = Y_n^	op \mathbb{E}[Y_n'] = 0$. With $
abla g = (1/\mathrm{tr}\Sigma_f, 0)$ at $(0, \mathrm{tr}\Sigma_f)$, only the $Z_n$ variance contributes: $
abla g^	op \Sigma_T 
abla g = \mathrm{tr}(\Sigma_f^2)/(\mathrm{tr}\Sigma_f)^2 = 1/d_{\mathrm{eff}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Off-diagonal covariance vanishes; variance is $1/d_{eff}$.
nodes.section: B.8 Variance-Scale Stopping Rule for Lag-$\tau$ Coupling

nodes.name: Participation ratio
nodes.statement: Equivalently, $\mathrm{Var}[\hat\rho(\tau)] \approx 1/(N d_{\mathrm{eff}})$ to leading order, with denominator fluctuations contributing only at $o(1/N)$. The quantity $d_{\mathrm{eff}} \in [1, d]$ is the participation ratio of the eigenvalues of $\Sigma_f$: it equals $d$ when $\Sigma_f$ is isotropic and drops toward $1$ as the spectrum concentrates on a single direction.
nodes.statement_short: Variance $\approx 1/(Nd_{eff})$ with $d_{eff}\in[1,d]$.
nodes.section: B.8 Variance-Scale Stopping Rule for Lag-$\tau$ Coupling

nodes.name: Factor out the dominant exponential
nodes.statement: Starting from Lemma~\ref{lem:spectral}(i), factor out the dominant exponential: \[ C(\tau) = e^{-\mu_2 \tau}\bigg[\underbrace{\alpha_2 \alpha_2^\top}_{M} + \underbrace{\sum_{k \geq 3} e^{-(\mu_k - \mu_2)\tau}\, \alpha_k \alpha_k^\top}_{R(\tau)}\bigg]. \]
nodes.statement_short: Write $C(\tau)$ as $e^{-\mu_2\tau}$ times rank-one plus remainder.

nodes.name: Remainder bound
nodes.statement: Since $\mu_k \geq \mu_3$ for all $k \geq 3$, the remainder satisfies $\|R(\tau)\| \leq e^{-(\mu_3 - \mu_2)\tau} \sum_{k \geq 3} \|\alpha_k\|^2$. The prefactor $e^{-\mu_2 \tau}$ does not affect eigenvectors, so $v_1(\tau)$ is the leading eigenvector of $M + R(\tau)$ where $M = \alpha_2 \alpha_2^\top$ is rank-one with eigenvalue $\|\alpha_2\|^2$ and eigenvector $\alpha_2/\|\alpha_2\|$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the remainder by $e^{-(\mu_3-\mu_2)\tau}$.

nodes.name: Davis-Kahan
nodes.statement: For sufficiently large $\tau$, $\|R(\tau)\| < \|\alpha_2\|^2$, so the leading eigenvalue of $M$ is separated from all eigenvalues of $M + R(\tau)$ outside a neighborhood of $\|\alpha_2\|^2$ by a gap of at least $\|\alpha_2\|^2 - \|R(\tau)\|$. By the Davis--Kahan $\sin\Theta$ theorem, the unit-norm eigenvector $v_1(\tau)$ satisfies \[ 1 - \frac{\langle v_1(\tau),\, \alpha_2\rangle^2}{\|\alpha_2\|^2} \;\leq\; \left(\frac{\|R(\tau)\|}{\|\alpha_2\|^2 - \|R(\tau)\|}\right)^2. \]
nodes.statement_short: Eigengap and Davis-Kahan bound the angle.

nodes.name: Rate
nodes.statement: As $\tau \to \infty$, $\|R(\tau)\| \to 0$ and the denominator approaches the constant $\|\alpha_2\|^2$, so the bound is $O(e^{-2(\mu_3 - \mu_2)\tau})$.
nodes.statement_short: The bound decays as $e^{-2(\mu_3-\mu_2)\tau}$.

nodes.name: Subspace convergence
nodes.statement: The same factorization extends to subspace level. Fix $m \geq 1$ and assume $\mu_{m+1} < \mu_{m+2}$ and that $\alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_{m+1}$ are linearly independent. Linear independence at fixed $m$ implies a positive lower bound on the $m$-th eigenvalue of the slow block, $\lambda_m\bigl(A_m(\tau)\bigr) \geq c_m\,e^{-(\mu_{m+1} - \mu_2)\tau}$ for some $c_m > 0$, where $A_m(\tau) = \sum_{k=2}^{m+1} e^{-(\mu_k - \mu_2)\tau}\,\alpha_k\alpha_k^\top$. Splitting the bracket into this slow block and a tail $R_m(\tau) = \sum_{k \geq m+2} e^{-(\mu_k - \mu_2)\tau}\,\alpha_k\alpha_k^\top$ with $\|R_m(\tau)\| \leq e^{-(\mu_{m+2} - \mu_2)\tau}\sum_{k \geq m+2}\|\alpha_k\|^2$. Applying the Davis--Kahan $\sin\Theta$ theorem to the gap between the top-$m$ block of $A_m(\tau)$ and the tail gives \[ \|V_m(\tau)V_m(\tau)^\top - \Pi_m\|_F^2 \;=\; O\bigl(e^{-2(\mu_{m+2} - \mu_{m+1})\tau}\bigr), \] where $V_m(\tau) \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times m}$ collects the top $m$ unit-norm eigenvectors of $C(\tau)$ and $\Pi_m$ is the orthogonal projector onto $\mathrm{span}(\alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_{m+1})$. The bound controls the \emph{subspace} only; identifying the individual eigenvectors $v_2(\tau), \ldots, v_m(\tau)$ with specific $\alpha_k$ requires additional gap and non-collinearity conditions on $\{\alpha_k\}$ that do not hold in general (the $\{\alpha_k\}$ are projection coefficients of coordinate functions onto the eigenfunctions $\{\psi_k\}$ and are not orthogonal). The bimodal case (Appendix~\ref{app:bimodal_heuristic}) is a special case where only $\alpha_2$ is non-negligible, so DA1 identifies cleanly. We validate per-direction recovery in the multi-direction regime empirically (Section~\ref{sec:exp_molecular}, Appendix~\ref{app:validation}).
nodes.statement_short: Same argument for the top-m block.

nodes.name: Slow block
nodes.statement: The same factorization extends to subspace level. Fix $m \geq 1$ and assume $\mu_{m+1} < \mu_{m+2}$ and that $\alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_{m+1}$ are linearly independent. Linear independence at fixed $m$ implies a positive lower bound on the $m$-th eigenvalue of the slow block, $\lambda_m\bigl(A_m(\tau)\bigr) \geq c_m\,e^{-(\mu_{m+1} - \mu_2)\tau}$ for some $c_m > 0$, where $A_m(\tau) = \sum_{k=2}^{m+1} e^{-(\mu_k - \mu_2)\tau}\,\alpha_k\alpha_k^\top$.
nodes.statement_short: Linear independence lower-bounds the slow block's m-th eigenvalue.

nodes.name: Tail bound
nodes.statement: Splitting the bracket into this slow block and a tail $R_m(\tau) = \sum_{k \geq m+2} e^{-(\mu_k - \mu_2)\tau}\,\alpha_k\alpha_k^\top$ with $\|R_m(\tau)\| \leq e^{-(\mu_{m+2} - \mu_2)\tau}\sum_{k \geq m+2}\|\alpha_k\|^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the tail.

nodes.name: Davis-Kahan for subspaces
nodes.statement: Applying the Davis--Kahan $\sin\Theta$ theorem to the gap between the top-$m$ block of $A_m(\tau)$ and the tail gives \[ \|V_m(\tau)V_m(\tau)^\top - \Pi_m\|_F^2 \;=\; O\bigl(e^{-2(\mu_{m+2} - \mu_{m+1})\tau}\bigr), \] where $V_m(\tau) \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times m}$ collects the top $m$ unit-norm eigenvectors of $C(\tau)$ and $\Pi_m$ is the orthogonal projector onto $\mathrm{span}(\alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_{m+1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Davis-Kahan gives the projector bound.

nodes.name: Limits of the bound
nodes.statement: The bound controls the \emph{subspace} only; identifying the individual eigenvectors $v_2(\tau), \ldots, v_m(\tau)$ with specific $\alpha_k$ requires additional gap and non-collinearity conditions on $\{\alpha_k\}$ that do not hold in general (the $\{\alpha_k\}$ are projection coefficients of coordinate functions onto the eigenfunctions $\{\psi_k\}$ and are not orthogonal). The bimodal case (Appendix~\ref{app:bimodal_heuristic}) is a special case where only $\alpha_2$ is non-negligible, so DA1 identifies cleanly. We validate per-direction recovery in the multi-direction regime empirically (Section~\ref{sec:exp_molecular}, Appendix~\ref{app:validation}).
nodes.statement_short: Individual eigenvectors are not identified; checked empirically.

nodes.name: Two-basin mixture
nodes.statement: Let $f = \pi_A f_A + \pi_B f_B$ where $f_A, f_B$ are localized around $\mu_A, \mu_B$ with negligible overlap, and $\pi_A, \pi_B$ are the basin masses. Write $A$ and $B$ for the two basins (the regions of support of $f_A$ and $f_B$, respectively).
nodes.statement_short: Set up a two-basin mixture.

nodes.name: Piecewise-constant psi_2
nodes.statement: In the strongly metastable limit, the slowest eigenfunction of the generator $\mathcal{L}_f$ is approximately piecewise constant on the two basins~\cite{Pavliotis2014}: \[ \psi_2(x) \approx \begin{cases} c_A & x \in A, \\ c_B & x \in B, \end{cases} \] with a thin transition region across the barrier. The intuition is that $\psi_2$ must be the slowest-relaxing observable under the dynamics; any function varying within a basin relaxes quickly (intra-basin mixing is fast), so the slowest observable is the one that distinguishes the two basins and is otherwise constant.
nodes.statement_short: The slowest eigenfunction is approximately constant on each basin (cited).

nodes.name: Levels by orthogonality
nodes.statement: Since $\psi_1 \equiv 1$ and $\langle \psi_1, \psi_2 \rangle_f = 0$, \[ \int \psi_2(x)\,f(x)\,dx = \pi_A c_A + \pi_B c_B = 0, \] so $c_B = -(\pi_A/\pi_B)\,c_A$. For equal weights ($\pi_A = \pi_B = 1/2$), this reduces to $c_B = -c_A$; write $c := c_A$.
nodes.statement_short: Orthogonality to constants fixes the two levels.

nodes.name: Compute alpha_2
nodes.statement: By definition, $(\alpha_2)_j = \int (x_j - (\bar x_f)_j)\,\psi_2(x)\,f(x)\,dx$. Splitting the integral over the two basins and using the piecewise-constant approximation, \[ \alpha_2 \approx c \int_A (x - \bar x_f)\,f(x)\,dx - c \int_B (x - \bar x_f)\,f(x)\,dx = c\bigl[\pi_A(\mu_A - \bar x_f) - \pi_B(\mu_B - \bar x_f)\bigr], \] where $\mu_A := \mathbb{E}_{f_A}[X]$ and analogously for $\mu_B$. For equal weights, $\bar x_f = (\mu_A + \mu_B)/2$, so $\mu_A - \bar x_f = \tfrac{1}{2}(\mu_A - \mu_B)$ and $\mu_B - \bar x_f = -\tfrac{1}{2}(\mu_A - \mu_B)$, giving \[ \alpha_2 \approx \tfrac{c}{2}(\mu_A - \mu_B). \]
nodes.statement_short: Split the integral over basins.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: That is, $\alpha_2$ is aligned with the vector connecting the two mode centers. For unequal weights, the same computation gives $\alpha_2 \propto \mu_A - \mu_B$ with a prefactor depending on $\pi_A, \pi_B$.
nodes.statement_short: $\alpha_2$ points along $\mu_A-\mu_B$.

nodes.name: Outline
nodes.statement: This appendix proves Theorem~\ref{thm:limit-spectrum} in three steps: (i) a finite-$N$ decomposition of $\hat C^{\mathrm{sym}}(\tau)$ as a weighted difference of two independent Wishart matrices (Section~\ref{app:wishart-decomp}); (ii) a short primer on the free-probability tools we use (Section~\ref{app:fp-primer}); (iii) the derivation of the Stieltjes cubic and edge quartic from the free-probability calculation (Section~\ref{app:polynomial-derivation}). Boundary cases ($\tau = 0, \tau = \infty$) and the small-$\gamma$ semicircle approximation are collected in Section~\ref{app:consequences}; scope and empirical verification in Section~\ref{app:scope}.
nodes.statement_short: Outline of the three-step proof.
nodes.section: C.4 Proof of Theorem~2: exact null spectrum of $\hat C^{\mathrm{sym}}(\tau)$

nodes.name: Estimator scope
nodes.statement: The proof analyses the simple-pair estimator $(1/N)\sum_n X_0^{(n)}(X_\tau^{(n)})^\top$, with $\gamma = d/N$ in the proportional limit. The trajectory-averaged form~\eqref{eq:c_hat_def} used in Algorithm~\ref{alg:ssa_da} pools $N(T+1-\tau)$ overlapping pairs that are dependent across $t$; we use the analytic edge as a reference floor for that estimator and rely on matched Monte-Carlo calibration when the pipeline departs from the exact simple-pair null.
nodes.statement_short: The proof is for the simple-pair estimator only.
nodes.section: C.4 Proof of Theorem~2: exact null spectrum of $\hat C^{\mathrm{sym}}(\tau)$

nodes.name: Why a rotation is needed
nodes.statement: The first step is a finite-$N$ rewriting of $\hat C^{\mathrm{sym}}(\tau))$ that converts it into a sum of functions of two \emph{independent} Gaussian ensembles. Contrast with the naive decomposition $\hat C(\tau) = e^{-\tau/2}\hat C(0) + \sigma\sqrt{1-e^{-\tau}}\,\hat R$ with $\hat R = N^{-1}\sum_n \xi^{(n)}(X_0^{(n)})^\top$: the two terms on the right share $X_0$ and are therefore \emph{not} independent, which is what prevents a clean application of free probability. Symmetrizing and rotating in a well-chosen $2{\times}2$ basis produces an independent-ensemble representation.
nodes.statement_short: The naive decomposition shares $X_0$; a rotation gives independent ensembles.

nodes.name: Lemma 2 and its proof
nodes.statement: \begin{lemma}[Exact decomposition of $\hat C^{\mathrm{sym}}(\tau)$] With $c_\pm(\tau) = (\sigma^2/2)(1 \pm e^{-\tau/2})$, there exist $d\times N$ random matrices $U, V$ with i.i.d.\ $\mathcal N(0,1)$ entries, independent of each other, such that \begin{equation} \hat C^{\mathrm{sym}}(\tau) \;=\; c_+(\tau)\,\frac{UU^\top}{N} \;-\; c_-(\tau)\,\frac{VV^\top}{N}. \end{equation} Equivalently, in distribution, $\hat C^{\mathrm{sym}}(\tau) \stackrel{d}{=} c_+(\tau)\,W_+ - c_-(\tau)\,W_-$, with $W_+,W_-$ i.i.d.\ $d\times d$ standard Wishart matrices at aspect ratio $\gamma = d/N$. Moreover, $(U, V)$ is obtained from $(\tilde X, Z)$ (standardized samples and noise, defined in the proof) by a specific orthogonal transformation applied column-wise, with angle a function of $\tau$ alone. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Standardize $X_0^{(n)} = \sigma\tilde X^{(n)}$ with $\tilde X^{(n)} \sim \mathcal N(0, I_d)$. Let $\xi^{(n)} \sim \mathcal N(0, I_d)$ be the OU noise column driving $X_\tau^{(n)} = \alpha\sigma \tilde X^{(n)} + \beta\, \xi^{(n)}$, where $\alpha = e^{-\tau/2}$ and $\beta = \sigma\sqrt{1 - e^{-\tau}}$; we write $\tilde X, Z$ for the $d \times N$ matrices whose $n$-th columns are $\tilde X^{(n)}, \xi^{(n)}$ (respectively). Then \[ 2N\,\hat C^{\mathrm{sym}}(\tau) \;=\; 2\alpha\sigma^2\,\tilde X\tilde X^\top \;+\; \beta\sigma\bigl(Z\tilde X^\top + \tilde X Z^\top\bigr). \] \emph{Intermediate change of basis.} Set $A = (Z + \tilde X)/\sqrt 2$ and $B = (Z - \tilde X)/\sqrt 2$. The $2\times 2$ transformation $(\tilde X, Z) \mapsto (A, B)$ is orthogonal, so $(A, B)$ has the same joint i.i.d.\ $\mathcal N(0, I_d)$ distribution as $(\tilde X, Z)$, with columns of $A$ and $B$ independent of one another. Then $\tilde X = (A - B)/\sqrt 2$ and $Z = (A + B)/\sqrt 2$, so direct expansion gives $\tilde X\tilde X^\top = \tfrac12(AA^\top + BB^\top - AB^\top - BA^\top)$ and $Z\tilde X^\top + \tilde X Z^\top = AA^\top - BB^\top$, so \[ 2N\,\hat C^{\mathrm{sym}}(\tau) \;=\; \underbrace{(\alpha\sigma^2 + \beta\sigma)}_{P}\,AA^\top \;+\; \underbrace{(\alpha\sigma^2 - \beta\sigma)}_{Q}\,BB^\top \;+\; \underbrace{(-\alpha\sigma^2)}_{R}\bigl(AB^\top + BA^\top\bigr). \] \emph{Diagonalization.} The $2{\times}2$ coefficient matrix $K = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}P&R\\mathbb{R}&Q\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ has eigenvalues $\tfrac{P+Q}{2} \pm \sqrt{\bigl(\tfrac{P-Q}{2}\bigr)^2 + R^2} = \alpha\sigma^2 \pm \sigma\sqrt{\alpha^2\sigma^2 + \beta^2} = \sigma^2(\alpha \pm 1)$ (using $\alpha^2\sigma^2 + \beta^2 = \sigma^2$). Let $O(\tau)$ be the orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix that diagonalizes $K$; its angle $\theta(\tau)$ satisfies $\tan 2\theta = 2R/(P-Q) = -\alpha\sigma/\beta = -e^{-\tau/2}/\sqrt{1 - e^{-\tau}}$, a function of $\tau$ alone. Applying $O(\tau)$ column-wise to the pair $(A_n, B_n)$ produces new $d \times N$ random matrices $(U, V)$. Since each column-pair $(A_n, B_n)$ is jointly i.i.d.\ $\mathcal N(0, I_{2d})$ and orthogonal transformations preserve the i.i.d.\ Gaussian distribution, $(U, V)$ are still jointly i.i.d.\ $\mathcal N(0, I_d)$ with columns of $U$ and $V$ independent of one another, and \[ 2N\,\hat C^{\mathrm{sym}}(\tau) \;=\; \sigma^2(1 + \alpha)\,UU^\top \;-\; \sigma^2(1 - \alpha)\,VV^\top. \] Dividing by $2N$ gives \eqref{eq:wishart-decomp}. Composing the two rotations, $(U, V)$ is obtained from $(\tilde X, Z)$ by a single orthogonal transformation with angle $\pi/4 + \theta(\tau)$, a deterministic function of $\tau$. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: State and prove the exact decomposition.

nodes.name: Standardize
nodes.statement: Standardize $X_0^{(n)} = \sigma\tilde X^{(n)}$ with $\tilde X^{(n)} \sim \mathcal N(0, I_d)$. Let $\xi^{(n)} \sim \mathcal N(0, I_d)$ be the OU noise column driving $X_\tau^{(n)} = \alpha\sigma \tilde X^{(n)} + \beta\, \xi^{(n)}$, where $\alpha = e^{-\tau/2}$ and $\beta = \sigma\sqrt{1 - e^{-\tau}}$; we write $\tilde X, Z$ for the $d \times N$ matrices whose $n$-th columns are $\tilde X^{(n)}, \xi^{(n)}$ (respectively). Then \[ 2N\,\hat C^{\mathrm{sym}}(\tau) \;=\; 2\alpha\sigma^2\,\tilde X\tilde X^\top \;+\; \beta\sigma\bigl(Z\tilde X^\top + \tilde X Z^\top\bigr). \]
nodes.statement_short: Write $2N\hat C^{sym}$ in standardized sample and noise matrices.

nodes.name: 45-degree rotation
nodes.statement: \emph{Intermediate change of basis.} Set $A = (Z + \tilde X)/\sqrt 2$ and $B = (Z - \tilde X)/\sqrt 2$. The $2\times 2$ transformation $(\tilde X, Z) \mapsto (A, B)$ is orthogonal, so $(A, B)$ has the same joint i.i.d.\ $\mathcal N(0, I_d)$ distribution as $(\tilde X, Z)$, with columns of $A$ and $B$ independent of one another. Then $\tilde X = (A - B)/\sqrt 2$ and $Z = (A + B)/\sqrt 2$, so direct expansion gives $\tilde X\tilde X^\top = \tfrac12(AA^\top + BB^\top - AB^\top - BA^\top)$ and $Z\tilde X^\top + \tilde X Z^\top = AA^\top - BB^\top$, so \[ 2N\,\hat C^{\mathrm{sym}}(\tau) \;=\; \underbrace{(\alpha\sigma^2 + \beta\sigma)}_{P}\,AA^\top \;+\; \underbrace{(\alpha\sigma^2 - \beta\sigma)}_{Q}\,BB^\top \;+\; \underbrace{(-\alpha\sigma^2)}_{R}\bigl(AB^\top + BA^\top\bigr). \]
nodes.statement_short: Rotate to $A,B$ and expand.

nodes.name: Diagonalize
nodes.statement: \emph{Diagonalization.} The $2{\times}2$ coefficient matrix $K = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}P&R\\mathbb{R}&Q\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ has eigenvalues $\tfrac{P+Q}{2} \pm \sqrt{\bigl(\tfrac{P-Q}{2}\bigr)^2 + R^2} = \alpha\sigma^2 \pm \sigma\sqrt{\alpha^2\sigma^2 + \beta^2} = \sigma^2(\alpha \pm 1)$ (using $\alpha^2\sigma^2 + \beta^2 = \sigma^2$). Let $O(\tau)$ be the orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix that diagonalizes $K$; its angle $\theta(\tau)$ satisfies $\tan 2\theta = 2R/(P-Q) = -\alpha\sigma/\beta = -e^{-\tau/2}/\sqrt{1 - e^{-\tau}}$, a function of $\tau$ alone. Applying $O(\tau)$ column-wise to the pair $(A_n, B_n)$ produces new $d \times N$ random matrices $(U, V)$. Since each column-pair $(A_n, B_n)$ is jointly i.i.d.\ $\mathcal N(0, I_{2d})$ and orthogonal transformations preserve the i.i.d.\ Gaussian distribution, $(U, V)$ are still jointly i.i.d.\ $\mathcal N(0, I_d)$ with columns of $U$ and $V$ independent of one another, and \[ 2N\,\hat C^{\mathrm{sym}}(\tau) \;=\; \sigma^2(1 + \alpha)\,UU^\top \;-\; \sigma^2(1 - \alpha)\,VV^\top. \] Dividing by $2N$ gives \eqref{eq:wishart-decomp}. Composing the two rotations, $(U, V)$ is obtained from $(\tilde X, Z)$ by a single orthogonal transformation with angle $\pi/4 + \theta(\tau)$, a deterministic function of $\tau$.
nodes.statement_short: Diagonalize the 2x2 coefficient matrix to get $U,V$.

nodes.name: Asymptotic freeness
nodes.statement: $W_+, W_-$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:decomp} are independent standard Wisharts with i.i.d.\ $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ entries, each orthogonally invariant in distribution. By Voiculescu's asymptotic-freeness theorem for Gaussian ensembles~\cite{voiculescu1992,nica2006}, they become asymptotically free as $d\to\infty$ with $d/N \to \gamma \in (0, \infty)$.
nodes.statement_short: Independent orthogonally invariant Wisharts are asymptotically free.
nodes.section: C.4.2 Step 2: primer on free additive convolution and the $R$-transform

nodes.name: R-transform of the limit
nodes.statement: Consequently $\mathrm{ESD}(\hat C^{\mathrm{sym}}(\tau))$ converges weakly almost surely to $\mu_\tau^\gamma = (c_+\,\mathrm{MP}(\gamma)) \boxplus (-c_-\,\mathrm{MP}(\gamma))$, and \begin{equation} R_{\mu_\tau^\gamma}(z) \;=\; \frac{c_+}{1 - c_+\gamma z} \;-\; \frac{c_-}{1 + c_-\gamma z}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The limit is a free convolution with explicit R-transform.
nodes.section: C.4.2 Step 2: primer on free additive convolution and the $R$-transform

nodes.name: MP atom
nodes.statement: The standard Marchenko--Pastur measure $\mathrm{MP}(\gamma)$ has a point mass $\max(0, 1-1/\gamma)$ at the origin, arising from the rank deficiency of the Wishart matrix when $d > N$~\cite{marchenko1967, bai2010}.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the MP atom.
nodes.section: C.4.2 Step 2: primer on free additive convolution and the $R$-transform

nodes.name: Atom rule
nodes.statement: Free additive convolution combines atoms via the rule \cite{nica2006}: if $\mu$ has atom of mass $p$ at $a$ and $\nu$ has atom of mass $q$ at $b$, then $\mu \boxplus \nu$ has atom of mass $\max(0, p + q - 1)$ at $a + b$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the free-convolution atom rule (cited).
nodes.section: C.4.2 Step 2: primer on free additive convolution and the $R$-transform

nodes.name: Atom mass
nodes.statement: Applied to $(c_+\,\mathrm{MP}(\gamma)) \boxplus (-c_-\,\mathrm{MP}(\gamma))$ — both atoms at $0$ with mass $1 - 1/\gamma$ for $\gamma > 1$ — the result has an atom at $0$ of mass $\max(0, 2(1 - 1/\gamma) - 1) = \max(0, 1 - 2/\gamma)$. The continuous part has the complementary mass $\min(1, 2/\gamma)$ and remains characterized by the Stieltjes cubic and edge quartic derived below; the $R$-transform identity~\eqref{eq:R-explicit-appendix} continues to hold for all $\gamma > 0$.
nodes.statement_short: The atom has mass $\max(0,1-2/\gamma)$.
nodes.section: C.4.2 Step 2: primer on free additive convolution and the $R$-transform

nodes.name: Validity for all gamma
nodes.statement: The formal identity $R_{\mathrm{MP}(\gamma)}(z) = 1/(1-\gamma z)$ is valid as a generating function regardless of $\gamma$: for $\gamma \le 1$ it inverts to the absolutely continuous MP density on $[(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2, (1+\sqrt\gamma)^2]$; for $\gamma > 1$ the same formal $R$ inverts via the Stieltjes transform $G(z) = m/z + h(z)$ to a measure with an atom of mass $m = 1 - 1/\gamma$ at $0$, with the atom emerging because $G_\mu$ acquires a residue at $z = 0$. This recovers the decomposition \eqref{eq:mu_tau_decomp} of Theorem~\ref{thm:limit-spectrum}.
nodes.statement_short: The formal R-transform is valid for every $\gamma$; recovers the decomposition.
nodes.section: C.4.2 Step 2: primer on free additive convolution and the $R$-transform

nodes.name: Finite-N rank check
nodes.statement: The rank-deficiency argument has a direct finite-$N$ counterpart: $\hat C^{\mathrm{sym}}(\tau)$ has rank at most $2N$ (it is a sum of $N$ symmetric outer products on $\mathrm{span}(X_t, X_{t+\tau})$), so when $d > 2N$ exactly $d - 2N$ eigenvalues are deterministically zero, and the empirical atom mass $(d - 2N)/d \to 1 - 2/\gamma$ matches the free-conv prediction. The same atom mass can be obtained directly from the cubic Stieltjes equation~\eqref{eq:stieltjes-cubic} by a dominant-balance argument at $z = 0$ (not shown).
nodes.statement_short: Rank at most 2N matches the atom mass.
nodes.section: C.4.2 Step 2: primer on free additive convolution and the $R$-transform

nodes.name: Inverse identity
nodes.statement: The compositional-inverse identity $K(G(\lambda)) = \lambda$ with $K = R + 1/z$ and \eqref{eq:R-explicit-appendix} yields, writing $G = G(\lambda)$, \[ \frac{c_+}{1 - c_+\gamma G} \;-\; \frac{c_-}{1 + c_-\gamma G} \;+\; \frac{1}{G} \;=\; \lambda. \]
nodes.statement_short: Write $K(G)=\lambda$ explicitly.
nodes.section: C.4.3 Step 3: polynomial equations via the $R$-transform

nodes.name: Cubic
nodes.statement: Multiplying through by $G(1 - c_+\gamma G)(1 + c_-\gamma G)$ and collecting terms polynomial in $G$ gives the cubic \eqref{eq:stieltjes-cubic} of Theorem~\ref{thm:limit-spectrum}. The leading $G^3$ term comes from the product of the two denominators times $\lambda G$; the $G^2$ coefficient collects cross terms and simplifies to $\gamma[c_+c_-(2-\gamma) + \lambda(c_+ - c_-)]$; the $G^1$ coefficient reduces to $(c_+ - c_-)(1-\gamma) - \lambda$; and the constant term is $1$.
nodes.statement_short: Clear denominators: the Stieltjes cubic.
nodes.section: C.4.3 Step 3: polynomial equations via the $R$-transform

nodes.name: Density
nodes.statement: Density on the interior of the support follows from Sokhotski--Plemelj~\cite{bai2010}: $\mathrm{Im}\,G(\lambda + i0^+) = -\pi\rho(\lambda)$.
nodes.statement_short: Sokhotski-Plemelj gives the density.
nodes.section: C.4.3 Step 3: polynomial equations via the $R$-transform

nodes.name: Edges as discriminant zeros
nodes.statement: Edges are points at which the complex-conjugate pair of roots of the cubic \eqref{eq:stieltjes-cubic} coalesces onto the real line as a double root. A cubic of the form $a G^3 + b G^2 + c G + 1$ (constant term $1$, leading coefficient $a$) has a double root iff its discriminant vanishes: $18abc - 4b^3 + b^2 c^2 - 4ac^3 - 27a^2 = 0$, which with $(a,b,c)$ from \eqref{eq:stieltjes-cubic} is precisely the quartic $\Delta_\tau(\lambda) = 0$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:limit-spectrum}(i).
nodes.statement_short: Edges are double roots: discriminant zero.
nodes.section: C.4.3 Step 3: polynomial equations via the $R$-transform

nodes.name: Leading coefficient
nodes.statement: Expanding as a polynomial in $\lambda$: each of $a, b, c$ is at most linear in $\lambda$, so the five summands have $\lambda$-degrees $(3, 3, 4, 4, 2)$. Writing $[\lambda^k] f$ for the coefficient of $\lambda^k$ in a polynomial $f$ (in $\lambda$), the $\lambda^4$ contribution is \[ [\lambda^4]\,\Delta_\tau \;=\; [\lambda^2]\,b^2 \cdot [\lambda^2]\,c^2 \;+\; (-4)\,[\lambda^1]\,a \cdot [\lambda^3]\,c^3 \;=\; \gamma^2(c_+\!-\!c_-)^2 + 4 c_+c_-\gamma^2 \;=\; \gamma^2(c_++c_-)^2 \;=\; \gamma^2\sigma^4, \] using $(c_+-c_-)^2 + 4 c_+c_- = (c_++c_-)^2$ and $c_++c_- = \sigma^2$.
nodes.statement_short: The quartic has leading coefficient $\gamma^2\sigma^4$.
nodes.section: C.4.3 Step 3: polynomial equations via the $R$-transform

nodes.name: Support structure
nodes.statement: Depending on $(\gamma, \tau)$, the quartic $\Delta_\tau$ may have two or four real roots. The real roots are precisely the candidate boundary points of the continuous support: in the one-cut regime only the smallest and largest real roots occur as support edges; in the supercritical regime $\gamma > 2$, four real roots occur and the support splits into two intervals around the atom at zero (Section~\ref{app:consequences}). The operational threshold $\lambda_+(\tau)$ is the largest real support edge.
nodes.statement_short: Two or four real roots: one or two support intervals.
nodes.section: C.4.3 Step 3: polynomial equations via the $R$-transform

nodes.name: Biquadratic
nodes.statement: $c_+ = c_- = c := \sigma^2/2$. The edge quartic becomes a biquadratic in $\lambda$: $\lambda^4 + c^2(1 - 10\gamma - 2\gamma^2)\lambda^2 - \gamma c^4(2-\gamma)^3 = 0$, with discriminant $(1+4\gamma)^3$.
nodes.statement_short: With $c_+=c_-$ the quartic is biquadratic.
nodes.section: C.4.4 Boundary cases and special regimes

nodes.name: Closed form
nodes.statement: Setting $s = \sqrt{1+4\gamma}$ and simplifying via $2-\gamma = (3-s)(3+s)/4$ and $s^4 + 8s^3 + 18s^2 - 27 = (s-1)(s+3)^3$, \begin{equation} \boxed{\;\lambda_+(\infty) \;=\; \frac{\sigma^2}{8}(s+3)^{3/2}\sqrt{s-1}, \qquad s = \sqrt{1+4\gamma},\;} \end{equation} and $\lambda_-(\infty) = -\lambda_+(\infty)$ by symmetry.
nodes.statement_short: Factor and take the positive root.
nodes.section: C.4.4 Boundary cases and special regimes

nodes.name: Dirichlet form
nodes.statement: The Dirichlet form associated with $\mathcal{L}_{A_0}$ is $\mathcal{E}_{A_0}(\varphi) = \tfrac{1}{2}\int (\nabla \varphi)^\top A_0 (\nabla \varphi)\,f\,dx$, defined on its natural domain $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{E}_{A_0}) \subset H^1(f\,dx) \cap L^2_0(f\,dx)$ of zero-mean functions.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the Dirichlet form.
nodes.section: D.1 Reversible It\^o Diffusions with Different Constant Diffusion Matrices

nodes.name: Pointwise comparison
nodes.statement:
For any test function $\varphi$ in this domain, \[ \lambda_{\min}\! igl(B^{-1/2} A B^{-1/2} igr)\,(
abla \varphi)^	op B (
abla \varphi) \;\le\; (
abla \varphi)^	op A (
abla \varphi) \;\le\; \lambda_{\max}\! igl(B^{-1/2} A B^{-1/2} igr)\,(
abla \varphi)^	op B (
abla \varphi) \] pointwise in $x$, by the variational characterization of $\lambda_{\min}, \lambda_{\max}$ of $B^{-1/2} A B^{-1/2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Compare the quadratic forms pointwise.
nodes.section: D.1 Reversible It\^o Diffusions with Different Constant Diffusion Matrices

nodes.name: Integrated comparison
nodes.statement: Integrating against $f\,dx$, \[ \lambda_{\min}\!\bigl(B^{-1/2} A B^{-1/2}\bigr)\,\mathcal{E}_B(\varphi) \;\le\; \mathcal{E}_A(\varphi) \;\le\; \lambda_{\max}\!\bigl(B^{-1/2} A B^{-1/2}\bigr)\,\mathcal{E}_B(\varphi). \]
nodes.statement_short: Integrate to compare Dirichlet forms.
nodes.section: D.1 Reversible It\^o Diffusions with Different Constant Diffusion Matrices

nodes.name: Min-max
nodes.statement: The min-max characterization of the $k$-th non-trivial eigenvalue, \[ \mu_k(A_0) \;=\; \min_{\substack{V_k \subset L^2_0(f\,dx) \\ \dim V_k = k}}\;\max_{\substack{\varphi \in V_k \\ \|\varphi\|_{L^2(f)} = 1}} \mathcal{E}_{A_0}(\varphi), \] applied with $A_0 = A$ and $A_0 = B$ then gives the stated bound term-by-term.
nodes.statement_short: Courant-Fischer transfers the bound to eigenvalues.
nodes.section: D.1 Reversible It\^o Diffusions with Different Constant Diffusion Matrices

nodes.name: Eyring-Kramers form
nodes.statement: The Eyring--Kramers form gives $\mu_k^{\rm UD}(\eta, \beta;\, f) \sim \kappa_k(\eta, M;\, f)\exp(-\beta \Delta U_k(f))$ as $\beta \to \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Eyring-Kramers asymptotics.

nodes.name: Ratio of rates
nodes.statement: Taking the ratio of the rates for $f_A$ and $f_B$, the prefactor ratio is finite and positive while the exponent diverges (in absolute value) as $\beta \to \infty$, so the sign of $\mu_k^{\rm UD}(f_A) - \mu_k^{\rm UD}(f_B)$ is determined by $\Delta U_k(f_B) - \Delta U_k(f_A)$ in the deep-barrier limit.
nodes.statement_short: Finite prefactor ratio, diverging exponent.

nodes.name: Overdamped case
nodes.statement: The same applies to $\mu_k^{\rm OD}$ via the Smoluchowski limit.
nodes.statement_short: Same for overdamped rates.

nodes.name: Forward process
nodes.statement: A diffusion model defines a forward noising process $q(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}(x_t; \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t} x_0, \sigma_t^2 I)$, where $\sigma_t^2 = 1 - \bar\alpha_t$. The marginal at time $t$ is \[ f_t(x) = \int q(x \mid x_0) f(x_0)\, dx_0. \]
nodes.statement_short: Forward noising kernel and marginal.

nodes.name: Score via posterior mean
nodes.statement: Using Bayes' rule to express the posterior $p(x_0 \mid x_t)$, the score of this marginal satisfies \[ \nabla \log f_t(x) = -\frac{x - \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_t = x]}{\sigma_t^2}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Bayes' rule: score through the posterior mean.

nodes.name: Reparameterization
nodes.statement: One can notice that any sample from this kernel can be written in the reparameterized form \[ x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sigma_t\,\epsilon, \qquad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), \] which isolates the structured signal $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0$ from the additive Gaussian noise $\sigma_t\,\epsilon$. Rearranging gives the residual noise explicitly: \[ \epsilon = \frac{x_t - \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0}{\sigma_t}, \qquad \text{equivalently,} \qquad x_0 = \frac{x_t - \sigma_t\,\epsilon}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Reparameterize the noised sample.

nodes.name: Denoiser estimate
nodes.statement: A diffusion model trains a denoiser $\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)$ to predict this noise $\epsilon$, so that $\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_t] \approx (x_t - \sigma_t\,\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t))/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}$.
nodes.statement_short: The denoiser estimates the posterior mean.

nodes.name: Tweedie identity
nodes.statement: Substituting into the score expression above yields the Tweedie identity: \[ \nabla \log f_t(x) = -\frac{\epsilon_\theta(x, t)}{\sigma_t}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Substitute to obtain the identity.

nodes.name: Add R-transforms
nodes.statement: By additivity, $R_\mu = R_A + R_B$.
nodes.statement_short: Add the R-transforms.
nodes.section: C.4.2 Step 2: primer on free additive convolution and the $R$-transform

nodes.name: Invert K
nodes.statement: Set $K_\mu(z) := R_\mu(z) + 1/z$. Then $G_\mu$, the Stieltjes transform of $\mu_A \boxplus \mu_B$, is the compositional inverse, defined implicitly by $K_\mu(G_\mu(z)) = z$. This is a polynomial equation in $G$; in our setting it is the \emph{Stieltjes cubic} (Section~\ref{app:polynomial-derivation}, Eq.~\eqref{eq:stieltjes-cubic}), so $G_\mu(z)$ is an algebraic function of $z$ given by Cardano's formula on the upper-half-plane branch.
nodes.statement_short: Invert $K$ to get the Stieltjes transform (cubic).
